en: The Source of the Dharma-System of the Mahāyāna, composed by Master Guāng.
Based on the Sarvāstivāda school, the sources of all dharmas are briefly of five kinds: first, form-dharmas; second, mind-dharmas.
There are five categories of phenomena: first, mental factors; second, formations dissociated from the mind;
third, unconditioned phenomena. Regarding the first, matter, there are briefly eleven types:
namely, (1) the eye, (2) the ear, (3) the nose, (4) the tongue, (5) the body, (6) visible form, (7) sound, (8) odor, (9) taste, (10) tangibility, and (11) non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Second, the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are briefly of one kind, namely the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
Third, the mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*) are briefly forty-six kinds:

the ten great ground factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome ground factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), the ten great afflictive ground factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*), the six great unwholesome ground factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*), the two minor afflictive ground factors (*parīttakleśabhūmika*), and the ten [unspecified] factors.

The indeterminate [mental factors] consist of eight; the universal ground-factors (mahābhūmika) consist of ten: first, feeling (vedanā); second, perception (saṃjñā); third, volition (cetanā); fourth, contact (sparśa);

fifth, desire (chanda); sixth, wisdom (prajñā); seventh, mindfulness (smṛti); eighth, attention (manaskāra); ninth, resolve (adhimokṣa); tenth, concentration (samādhi). The great wholesome ground-factors (kuśalamahābhūmika) consist of ten: first, faith (śraddhā); second, heedfulness (apramāda);
third, pliancy (praśrabdhi); fourth, equanimity (upekṣā); fifth, shame (hrī); sixth, dread of blame (apatrāpya); seventh, non-attachment (alobha); eighth, non-hatred (adveṣa).
The nine [mental factors] of non-harming and the ten of diligence; the six universal factors of great affliction (mahā-kleśa-bhūmika) are:
first, ignorance; second, negligence; third, laziness; fourth, lack of faith; fifth, torpor; and sixth, restlessness. The two universal factors of unwholesomeness (akuśala-mahābhūmika) are:
first, shamelessness; and second, lack of dread. The ten minor afflictive factors (parītta-kleśa-bhūmika) are: first, anger; second, concealment; third, avarice; fourth, envy; and fifth, resentment.

The six hindrances, the seven resentments, the eight forms of flattery, the nine deceptions, and the ten types of arrogance; furthermore, there are eight factors that are not fixed: first, vitarka (applied thought); second, vicāra (sustained thought); third, middha (drowsiness);
fourth, kaukṛtya (regret); fifth, rāga (attachment); sixth, pratigha (aversion); seventh, māna (pride); and eighth, vicikitsā (doubt).

The fourth category, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), briefly comprises fourteen types: (1) acquisition (*prāpti*), (2) non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), (3) homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*),

(4) the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedayita-vipāka*), (5) the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), (6) the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), (7) the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), (8) birth (*jāti*), (9) subsistence (*sthiti*),
(10) change (*jarā*), (11) dissolution (*anityatā*), (12) names (*nāman*), (13) phrases (*pada*), and (14) phonemes (*vyañjana*).

The fifth category, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), briefly consists of three types: first, space (*ākāśa*); second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Altogether, these constitute seventy-five phenomena that serve as the substance of all dharmas; one should reflect upon them well.
Within this, there are two parts: first, a brief presentation and explanation; second, an analysis through various categories.
Regarding the brief presentation and explanation:

the first is the category of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), which consists of eleven [factors] because they are subject to change and resistance (*rūpyate*). They are called "matter" (*rūpa*) because they arise from being changed and resisted. "Eye" refers to the internal sense base (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*).
The eye-consciousness has as its basis the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which is capable of seeing visible objects;
it is material, invisible, and resistant. This is explained in detail for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth as well.

"Matter" refers to the external sense-base (*bāhyāyatana*) which is seen by the eye, derived from the four great elements, material, visible, and resistant. There are twenty kinds of matter, namely: first, blue; second, yellow... [and so on].
1. Red; 2. White; 3. Long; 4. Short; 5. Square; 6. Circular; 7. High; 8. Low; 9. Regular; 10.
Irregular; 11. Clouds; 12. Smoke; 13. Dust; 14. Mist; 15. Shadow; 16. Light; 17. Radiance; 18. Darkness.
Sound refers to the external sense base which is heard by the ear and is derived from the four great elements.
There are eight kinds of sound that possess form, are invisible, and are resistant:
first, pleasant sounds produced by sentient beings caused by appropriated great elements, such as the pleasant voice uttered when speaking;

second, unpleasant sounds produced by sentient beings caused by appropriated great elements, such as the harsh voice uttered when speaking; third, [sounds] produced by non-sentient things caused by appropriated great elements...
1. Agreeable sound caused by appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*), which is not a sentient being, such as the pleasant sound of clapping hands; 2.
Disagreeable sound caused by appropriated great elements, which is not a sentient being, such as the unpleasant sound of clapping hands;

3. Agreeable sound caused by non-appropriated great elements, which is a sentient being, such as the pleasant sound of emanated speech; 4. [Disagreeable sound caused by non-appropriated great elements, which is a sentient being. (Note: Text fragment provided)

Unpleasant sounds, such as artificial speech or harsh voices, have the seven types of non-appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause and are not designated as belonging to sentient beings.
Pleasant sounds, such as external agreeable sounds, have the eight types of non-appropriated great elements as their cause and are not designated as belonging to sentient beings.

Unpleasant sounds, such as external disagreeable sounds, are likewise. As for odor, it refers to that which is smelled by the nose among the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), and is produced from the four great elements.
There are four types of odors that possess form, are invisible, and are resistant: namely, first, pleasant odor; second, unpleasant odor; third, equal odor; and fourth, unequal odor.
Alternatively, it is said there are three odors: first, pleasant odor; second, unpleasant odor; and third, neutral odor.

Odor is an external base (*bāhyāyatana*) that is tasted by the tongue and is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); it possesses form, is invisible, and is resistant. There are six [types] of this.

Regarding the types, there are six: first, sweet; second, sour; third, salty; fourth, pungent; fifth, bitter; and sixth, bland. Regarding the tangible objects (spraṣṭavya), they refer to external bases that are touched by the body;
these consist of the four great elements and the derived matter produced from the four great elements. This tangible matter is visible and resistant. There are eleven kinds of tangibles:
first, earth; second, water; third, fire; fourth, wind; fifth, smoothness; sixth, roughness; seventh, lightness; and eighth, heaviness.
Nine: cold; ten: hunger; eleven: thirst. Regarding what is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*):

although non-informative action has the nature of matter and karma like informative action (*vijñapti*), it does not manifest the internal goodness or evil of one's mind to others for them to understand; therefore, it is named "non-informative. Within this, there are two types:
first, the wholesome; second, the unwholesome. Within the wholesome, there are again two: first, that which arises from informative action; second, that which follows the movement of the mind.
Manifest karma is further divided into two types: first, that which is intermediate (*madhyama*), and second, the prātimokṣa. That which accords with the mind is also twofold:

first, that which is associated with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samprayukta*), namely impure (*sāsrava*) discipline; and second, that which is associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta*), namely pure (*anāsrava*) discipline. Within the unwholesome (*akuśala*), there are likewise two kinds:
first, intermediate discipline (*madhyama-śīla*), and second, bad discipline (*duḥśīla*).

The second category, mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), is sometimes called mind (*manas*) and sometimes called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because it accumulates and arises, it is called "mind" (*citta*); because it cogitates, it is called "mind" (*manas*);

and because it discerns, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). This refers to the seven elements of mind (*saptamanodhātu*), the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
The third category, the forty-six mental concomitants (*caitasika*), are those that belong to the mind and are thus called "mental factors. Among these, the great [universal]...

Regarding the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*): "ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to a sphere of activity. If this is the sphere of activity for that, then this is said to be the ground of that factor.

Because they are the ground of the great universal factors, they are called the "great ground" (*mahābhūmi*). Among these, if a factor belongs to the great ground, it is called a "universal mental factor" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
One should understand, according to the following examples, that this is a double *tatpuruṣa* compound: namely, these ten factors pervade all [consciousnesses].

"Mind-moment by mind-moment, what is experienced is called sensation (*vedanā*), which refers to the experiencing of suffering, pleasure, or that which is neither; perception (*saṃjñā*) refers to the grasping of specific characteristics within an object;

volition (*cetanā*) refers to that which enables the mind to engage in activity; contact (*sparśa*) refers to that which arises from the conjunction of faculty, object, and consciousness, and has the capacity for sensory encounter;

desire (*chanda*) refers to the longing for the tasks to be performed; wisdom (*prajñā*) refers to the capacity for discernment regarding phenomena; and mindfulness (*smṛti*) refers to clarity regarding the focal object."

*Smṛti* (mindfulness) refers to the mental application of not forgetting; *manasikāra* (attention) refers to that which causes the mind to be alert; *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction) refers to that which confirms an object; and *samādhi* (concentration) refers to one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding the ten *mahābhūmika-kuśala-dharmas* (great wholesome universal factors): "ground" (*bhūmi*) is as explained previously.

The term "great wholesome ground" (*mahākuśalabhūmi*) refers to the factors belonging to this ground, and these are called the "great wholesome universal factors" (*mahākuśalabhūmikadharma*). Among these, those factors that belong to the great wholesome ground are termed the great wholesome universal factors. This means:
These ten factors exist only in wholesome minds. "Faith" (śraddhā) refers to that which clarifies and purifies the mind, or the acceptance and assent toward the Truths and so forth.

"Diligence" (apramāda) refers to the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas. "Tranquility" (praśrabdhi) refers to the mind's state of pliancy. "Equanimity" (upekṣā) refers to the mind's state of impartiality and lack of agitation.

"Moral shame" (hrī) refers to feeling a sense of personal shame regarding the transgressions one has committed. "Moral dread" (apatrāpya) [refers to feeling shame regarding the transgressions one has committed] out of regard for others.
Regarding the shame felt toward the transgressions one has committed, "non-greed" means not being attached to objects; "non-hatred" means not being angry toward objects;
"non-harming" means the absence of injury or affliction; and "diligence" means having the nature of making the mind courageous and resolute.
If one relies on correct reasoning, the *Abhidharma*, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*’s final assessment (*viniścaya*), [these] constitute the great wholesome [factors].

Within the *mahābhūmika-dharmas*, it is further explained that there are "delight" (*abhinandanā*) and "aversion" (*vidveṣa*). Aversion refers to turning away from [an object], such as when taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as objects;

delight refers to leaning toward [an object], such as when taking cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as objects. Because these two do not arise simultaneously, the *Abhidharmakośa* does not include them among the universal mental factors.

Regarding the six *kleśamahābhūmika-dharmas*: "ground" (*bhūmi*) is explained as before. The ground of great afflictive factors is called the *kleśamahābhūmika*; herein, those factors which are great afflictions...

The factors belonging to the level of affliction (*kleśabhūmi*) are called the universal factors of great affliction (*mahā-kleśabhūmika-dharma*); these refer to the six factors that are always and exclusively present in defiled minds.
"Ignorance" (*avidyā*) means having delusion as its nature. "Heedlessness" (*pramāda*) means not cultivating wholesome qualities;
it is the factor opposed to the cultivation of all virtues. "Laziness" (*kausīdya*) means the mind lacking vigor; it is the factor opposed to the "diligence" (*vīrya*) mentioned previously.

Lack of faith (*aśraddhya*) refers to the mind not being clear and pure; it is the state opposed by the previously mentioned faith. Lethargy (*styāna*) refers to that which causes the mind to become heavy and dull.

Excitement (*auddhatya*) refers to that which causes the mind to be unpeaceful. Regarding the two "great unwholesome ground-dharmas" (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*): as for "ground" (*bhūmi*), it is explained as before.

The term "great unwholesome ground-dharma" means that those dharmas which belong to the great unwholesome ground are called "great unwholesome ground-dharmas. Among these, if a dharma is a great unwholesome...

Those factors belonging to the wholesome ground (*kuśala-bhūmi*) are called the "great unwholesome ground factors" (*akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*); that is to say, these two factors pervade only unwholesome minds.

*Ahrī* (lack of shame) means having no sense of shame when observing oneself regarding the transgressions one has committed; *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread) means having no sense of shame when observing others regarding the transgressions one has committed.

The ten factors of the minor affliction ground (*parītta-kleśabhūmi-dharma*)—the term "ground" (*bhūmi*) is explained as before—the name "minor affliction ground factors" refers to those factors of minor affliction that constitute a ground.

Regarding the "minor defilement ground" (*parīttakleśabhūmi*): herein, those factors that belong to the minor defilement ground are called the "minor defilement ground factors" (*parīttakleśabhūmikadharma*).
These ten factors are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), are associated with mental delusion (*moha*), and manifest individually.

*Krodha* (anger) is the arousal of the mind toward sentient or insentient objects, excluding hatred (*dveṣa*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*). *Mrakṣa* (concealment) is the hiding of one's own faults. *Mātsarya* (avarice) refers to stinginess regarding wealth or the Dharma.
*Styāna* (stolidity) refers to that which opposes generosity and causes the mind to be stingy and attached; *īrṣyā* (envy) means being displeased at the flourishing prosperity of others;
*daurmanasya* (dejection) refers to the stubborn adherence to sinful matters, by which one does not accept reasoned admonition;

*vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) refers to the ability to oppress others, by which one can carry out acts such as beating and reviling; and *upānāha* (resentment) refers to [the persistence] regarding the objects of anger.
"Repeatedly contemplating and not relinquishing enmity" refers to resentment (*upanāha*). "Deceit" (*śāṭhya*) refers to mental crookedness;

because of this, one cannot manifest oneself as one truly is, either by falsely denying reality or by employing expedients that cause others' understanding to be unclear. "Guile" (*māyā*) refers to deluding others.

"Arrogance" (*mada*) refers to being preceded by attachment to one's own qualities, which causes the mind to become heedless and devoid of regard for anything else. This is according to the *Nyāya* and the *Dharmaskandhapāda*.

In the discussion of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are many other types which, as appropriate, are all subsumed under anger (*krodha*) and the rest; alternatively, the intent of the treatise may differ, and thus they are not fixed.
Eighth, "indeterminate" refers to those that do not enter the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*); they are called the indeterminate factors of the ground (*aniyata-bhūmika-dharma*).

The indeterminate factors of the ground are explained as before: the basis of the indeterminate is called the indeterminate ground, and that which belongs to the indeterminate ground is [the indeterminate factor].

The factors of the non-concentrated stage (*asamāhita-bhūmika-dharma*) are as follows: *vitarka* (applied thought) is the coarse nature of the mind that seeks; *vicāra* (sustained thought) is the subtle nature of the mind that examines;
*middha* (sleep) has the nature of causing the mind to become obscure and withdrawn; *styāna* (torpor) is the lack of capacity to maintain the body;
*kaukṛtya* (remorse) is the nature of mental regret regarding an object of misconduct; *rāga* (attachment) is craving; *pratigha* (aversion) is resentment; *māna* (pride) is...
Doubt regarding the truths (*satya*)—defined as hesitation—is characterized by the nature of self-exaltation toward others.

According to the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the critical school (*viniścaya-vādins*), among the factors not fixed in their stage (*aniyata-bhūmika-dharma*), there is further mention of fear (*bhaya*). This exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in the higher realms, there is no fear.

Regarding the fear associated with revulsion (*nirveda*), some say it belongs to the category of afflictions (*kleśa-pakṣya*), while others say that fear extends to both the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Thus far.

The forty-six kinds of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) explained here are discussed based on the single system of the *Abhidharmakośa*. Question: Among the mental factors, why are there some that are presented as opposites (*pratipakṣa*) while others are not?

Answer: When evaluating the various sūtras and śāstras, the number of mental factors is not fixed. If one were to comprehensively search for and establish them through their mutual oppositions, [the list would expand].

However, [here we follow the *Kośa*]. *Note: The final sentence of the provided Chinese fragment appears incomplete, but the translation reflects the logical conclusion of the argument regarding the variability of mental factors across different texts.*
To avoid confusion, based on the *Abhidharmakośa*’s presentation of the definitions and their respective establishments, there are forty-six categories in total, as previously stated.

Among these forty-six, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), vitarka, vicāra, middha, and kaukṛtya—these fourteen—are not translated with distinct names because they may pertain to all three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral). Within the remaining thirty-two, there are in total...
The two categories consist of one pure class (*śuddha-pakṣa*) with ten members— namely, the twelve *mahā-bhūmika* dharmas— and one defiled class (*kliṣṭa-pakṣa*) with twenty-two members—
namely, the six *kleśa-mahābhūmika* dharmas, the six *akuśala-mahābhūmika* dharmas, the ten *parīttakleśabhūmika* dharmas,

as well as greed, hatred, pride, and doubt. If, within the defiled class, these five [mental factors] are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and pervade all six consciousnesses, they are then directly subsumed under the pure class.
If, within this, the five [mental factors] of abandonment are not pervasive across the six consciousnesses, they can only be translated as lateral counterparts and not as direct counterparts.
As for what are called direct counterparts, there are ten dharmas in total: the six great afflictive ground-dharmas and the two great unwholesome ground-dharmas, along with greed and hatred.
Among the six great afflictive ground-dharmas, ignorance (*moha*) is translated as non-delusion (*amoha*); non-delusion is precisely...

Within the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), because wisdom (*prajñā*) is already present, non-delusion (*amoha*) is not established as a separate factor among the wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*). Conversely, heedlessness (*pramāda*) is countered by diligence (*apramāda*);
laziness (*kausīdya*) by vigor (*vīrya*); lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) by faith (*śraddhā*); lethargy (*styāna*) by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); and restlessness (*auddhatya*) by equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Among the two unwholesome universal factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*), shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) is countered by shame (*hrī*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is countered by dread (*apatrāpya*). Regarding the [unwholesome] factors...
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), greed is transformed into non-greed and hatred into non-hatred.

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), although harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) does not extend to the five faculties of abandonment nor pervade all six consciousnesses, it is treated as a distinct transformation because its fault is so grave.

Even when a Bodhisattva is about to realize unsurpassed bodhi, if they still give rise to desire, malice, or harmful investigation, these faults are so severe that they obstruct the progress toward enlightenment.

Therefore, the other nine secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as pride (*māna*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), are translated differently because their meanings are not fixed; they can only be translated incidentally and not as primary translations.
This is because the other nine secondary afflictions and doubt do not pertain to all five stages of abandonment (*pañca-prahāṇa*) nor to all six consciousnesses (*ṣad-vijñāna*).

Although pride pertains to all five stages of abandonment, it does not pervade all six consciousnesses; thus, they are not translated [as primary terms]. These eleven types can only be translated incidentally.
Regarding the reversals, there are two types: first, reversal according to the gate of outflow (*niṣyanda*); second, reversal according to the gate of similarity in aspect (*ākāra*).

As for "reversal according to the gate of outflow," this means that because these are the outflowing fruits of the root afflictions: anger, resentment, and envy are the outflows of hatred (*dveṣa*), and thus they are reversed by the absence of hatred (*adveṣa*);

vexation (*pradāsa*) is the outflow of the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and thus it is reversed by the correct view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). As for the grasping at views being reversed by the correct view: [it is because] the grasping at views is taken as the correct view.

"View" (*dṛṣṭi*) is not established separately among the wholesome [factors] because it is already included within the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

"Concealment" (*mrakṣa*) is an outflow of greed (*lobha*); its opposite is included in non-greed (*alobha*), or it is an outflow of delusion (*moha*); its opposite is included in non-delusion (*amoha*), which is itself the factor of wisdom;

therefore, it is not established separately among the wholesome. Stinginess (*mātsarya*), deceit (*śāṭhya*), and arrogance (*mada*)—these three—are outflows of greed and are thus included [in non-greed].
Non-greed (*alobha*) and non-flattery (*amāyā*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of these [wholesome] views; conversely, [the opposites of] views are "wrong views" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Since right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is itself a factor of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is not established as wholesome by way of its outflow category alone. However, regarding the reversal [of the afflictions], nine [factors] are obtained. Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is a root affliction that is not an outflow; therefore, these two types are not reversed separately.
Although harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) is an outflow of anger (*krodha*), because its fault is particularly grave, it is reversed separately as previously explained.

The commentary states that regarding those factors whose mental aspects (*ākāra*) are similar to the opposites of the [three roots], for example: resentment (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and vexation (*pradāśa*) have mental aspects similar to hatred (*dveṣa*);

they are subsumed under non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Concealment (*mrakṣa*), if it is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of greed, has a mental aspect similar to greed (*lobha*) and is subsumed under non-greed (*alobha*).

If it is an outflow of delusion (*moha*), it has a mental aspect similar to delusion and is subsumed under non-delusion (*amoha*). Non-delusion is included within the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, the two types—avarice (*mātsarya*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*)—resemble the characteristics of greed (*lobha*) and are therefore subsumed under non-greed (*alobha*). Deceit (*śāṭhya*) refers to crookedness;
its opposite is rectitude (*rjju*), and since rectitude is equanimity (*upekṣā*), the *Prakaraṇapāda* explains equanimity as "rectitude of body and rectitude of mind.

As for arrogance (*mada*) and pride (*māna*): arrogance is self-conceit and indulgence, while pride is the looking down upon others and failing to respect teachers and elders. If one is not arrogant...
Pride (*māna*) is thus transformed into respect (*gaurava*), which is itself a form of shame (*hrī*). Doubt (*vicikitsā*) consists of a state of hesitation and indecisiveness;

if it can correctly resolve [the matter], it is transformed into wisdom (*prajñā*). Harm (*vihiṃsā*), although similar to anger (*krodha*), is a more serious fault and is separately categorized as explained previously.

The fourth category consists of the fourteen factors dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). They are called "dissociated from mind" because they do not associate with the mind; this distinguishes them from mental factors (*caitta*).

They are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*) because they belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which distinguishes them from matter (*rūpa*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Specifically, they are: 1. **Acquisition** (*prāpti*), which refers to the acquisition of those phenomena belonging to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*). 2. **Cessation through deliberation** (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). 3. **Cessation not through deliberation** (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). 4.

**Non-acquisition** (*aprāpti*), which refers to the non-acquisition of those phenomena belonging to sentient beings. (Note: The list of fourteen is traditionally expanded by including other categories such as *jāti*, *jarā*, *sthiti*, *anityatā*, *nāmakāya*, *padakāya*, and *vyañjanakāya*.)

Regarding the dharmas of number, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) refers to the mutual similarity of all sentient beings and the equality of their essential types;
thus it is named "homogeneity. Although its meaning is that of mutual similarity of essential types, it possesses multiple instances, such as the commonality of physical form;

hence it is also termed "homogeneity" in the sense of being a cause. It is called "homogeneity" because it is a shared portion (*sabhāga*) that serves as the common cause for those [beings]. There is no [other] homogeneity.

Regarding the maturation of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*): because those sentient beings do not give rise to the perception of duration for a long time during the interval of five hundred eons, it is called "non-perception.

This non-perception is itself the maturation, hence it is named the "maturation of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*). As for the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is so called because there is definitely no perception within that meditative state;
or alternatively, it is the "attainment of non-perception" because it is definitively designated as such. It functions by extinguishing a corresponding number of minds and mental factors.

There are as many factors present as constitute the essential nature of this meditative attainment; the "attainment of cessation" (nirodha-samāpatti) is so named because it is the total cessation of mind and mental factors.
Accordingly, as many mind and mental factors as cease, there are that many factors present which constitute the essential nature of this attainment.

Regarding the "life-faculty" (jīvitendriya): "life" refers to the life-span (*āyus*), and it is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) due to its predominance. As for "arising, abiding, change, and cessation": [in these]...

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that can cause [something] to arise is called "arising" (*jāti*); that which can maintain [it] is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); that which can cause it to decay is called "alteration" (*anyathātva*);

and that which can destroy it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*). These four are the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all conditioned phenomena. A "name" (*nāman*) refers to such designations as "devas" or "humans," which serve to designate various phenomena.

A "phrase" (*pada*) refers to expressions that fully convey meaning, such as the phrase "all conditioned formations are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*). A "syllable" (*vyañjana*) refers to phonemes such as *a*, *ā*, and so forth.
Names and phrases depend upon [the phonemes] and are able to manifest the meaning; thus, they manifest the meaning directly, while names and phrases manifest it indirectly.
Regarding the fifth category, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, there are three types. They are called "unconditioned" because they are produced without causes and conditions.

Space has non-obstruction as its nature; because it is non-obstructive, it accommodates all conditioned phenomena such as form. As for analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), "analysis" refers to...
Analytical cessation refers to *nirvāṇa*; because cessation is attained through analysis, it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

To whatever extent there are contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), to that same extent there is analytical cessation. Non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not attained by the power of analysis;

rather, it is simply the absence of conditions, and thus it is called non-analytical cessation. To whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), to that same extent there is non-analytical cessation. This is stated with respect to...
Although attainment (*prāpti*) exists in the future, its essential nature (*svabhāva*) actually extends across all three time periods.

Second, regarding the analysis by way of various categories, there are two parts: first, the inclusion within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); second, the analysis by way of various categories concerning the inclusion within the aggregates, bases, and elements.
As for the aggregates, they refer to the five aggregates; as for the bases, they refer to the twelve bases; and as for the elements, they refer to the eighteen elements.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*) refer to the meaning of a collection or assemblage of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), namely: form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The aggregate of form comprises eleven types of matter; the aggregates of feeling and perception comprise the two factors of feeling and perception from among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*);
and the aggregate of formations comprises fifty-eight factors, which consist of the forty-six mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*) excluding feeling and perception.
The remaining forty-four factors and the fourteen dissociated factors are subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Among the five aggregates, the first four are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the last one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because they are a collection of conditioned phenomena, they are all subsumed under the aggregates, whereas the unconditioned is not so subsumed because it is not a collection.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), these are: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
The meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) is the sense of being a gateway for the growth of taste, touch, and mental objects;

it is called a "base" because it is that which can produce the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). The bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, form, sound, odor, taste, and touch correspond respectively to the first ten of the eleven categories of form.
The base of the mind (*manāyatana*) is precisely the second [category], the sovereign mind, while the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) subsumes the remaining [categories] among those forms.

The forty-six mental factors (*caitta*), the fourteen formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute the sixty-four dharmas.

Regarding the eighteen realms (*dhātu*): the meaning of "realm" (*dhātu*) is the sense of a "lineage" (*gotra*) or "source. Within a single body, these consist of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental objects;
and the eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the eighteen realms.
Among these, there are eighteen classes of phenomena known as the eighteen *dhātus* (elements):

the elements of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility, which correspond respectively to the ten types of matter among the eleven categories of matter; the element of mind (*manodhātu*), and the six elements of consciousness (*ṣadvijñānadhātu*), which constitute the sovereign mind;
and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), as explained in the section on the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Second, regarding the analysis by way of various categories: briefly, the seventy-five dharmas are analyzed by means of one hundred categories.
Briefly, the analysis by way of two categories consists of seventeen types: matter and non-matter; visible and invisible; resistant and non-resistant; outflowing and non-outflowing;
conditioned and unconditioned; associated and dissociated; with superior and without superior; derived from the four great elements and not derived from the four.
The great derived [elements], the truths and non-truths, the appropriated and non-appropriated, the objective and non-objective,
the maturation and non-maturation, the view and non-view, the accumulation and non-accumulation, that which can cut and that which is cut,
the non-cutter and the non-cuttable, the faculties and non-faculties, and those with and without maturation— these are called "form" (rūpa) because they are susceptible to resistance (pratighāta).
That which is the opposite of this is called non-form (*arūpa*). Among the seventy-five dharmas, eleven are form:

the five sense faculties and the five objects are so called because they are subject to resistance (*sapratigha*); the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is so called because it arises from that which is resistant. The remaining sixty-four are non-form.
Regarding "visible" (*sanidarśana*) and "invisible" (*anidarśana*): that which is seen by the eye is called visible; that which is not seen by the eye is called invisible.

Among the seventy-five dharmas, matter (*rūpa*) is called visible, while the remaining seventy-four dharmas are called invisible. Although wisdom (*prajñā*) is also termed "seeing," here the definition is given specifically in relation to the eye.
Regarding "resistant" (*sapratigha*) and "non-resistant" (*apratigha*): it is so called because it possesses obstruction.

That which is termed "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) is the opposite of this; it is termed "without resistance" (*apratigha*). Among the seventy-five dharmas, the five faculties and the five objects are called "with resistance" because they are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*);
the remaining sixty-five dharmas are called "without resistance" because they are not composed of atoms.
Regarding "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*): "outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to leaking, namely the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because they increase in accordance with these outflows, they are called "with outflows. That which is contrary to this is called "without outflows. Among the eleven types of form (*rūpa*), non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) pertains to both categories.

If it is the morality concomitant with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*) or the non-informative form of the dispersed state (*vyutthita-avijñapti*), it is with outflows; if it is the morality concomitant with the Path (*mārga-samvara*), it is without outflows. The remaining ten types are [only] with outflows.

Regarding the categories [of dharmas], only those that are exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava) are as follows: among the forty-six mental factors (caitta), twenty-two—namely, the ten universal ground-dharmas (mahābhūmika), the ten wholesome ground-dharmas (kuśalamahābhūmika), and the two, vitarka and vicāra—pertain to both [types, with-outflows and without-outflows]. The remaining twenty-four are exclusively with-outflows.

Among the fourteen dissociated factors (viprayukta-saṃskāra), four—namely, acquisition (prāpti) and the three characteristics (lakṣaṇa)—pertain to both types; the remaining nine are exclusively with-outflows. The three unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) [dharmas]... [are without-outflows].

One should understand that the categories of "only outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), "with contention" (*saraṇa*), and "without contention" (*araṇa*) follow this same principle. Regarding "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*):

that which is produced by conditions is called conditioned; the opposite of this is called unconditioned. Among the seventy-five dharmas, the first seventy-two are conditioned, and the final three are unconditioned.
Regarding "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) and "dissociated" (*viprayukta*): these refer to [factors] that share the same time, basis, and activity.
Based on these five factors of equality, they are called "associated" (*samprayukta*).
They are associated because at one and the same moment, they share the same basis (sense faculty), the same mode of activity, the same object, and the same substance.
That which is contrary to this is called "dissociated" (*viprayukta*). Among the seventy-five dharmas, forty-seven types—consisting of the mind and mental factors—are associated.
The remaining twenty-eight should be understood as dissociated (*viprayukta*). Regarding "with superior" (*sottara*) and "without superior" (*anuttara*):

it is called "with superior" because there exists *nirvāṇa* as its superior; that which is contrary to this is called "without superior. Among the seventy-five dharmas, seventy-four are named "with superior," while *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) is named "without superior.
As for that which is derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which is not derived from the four great elements: [this refers to] their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
It is called "great" because it is vast; it is called "seed" because it can produce [other things]; and it is called "derived" because it arises from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

That which is contrary to this is called "non-derived from the four great elements. Among the seventy-five dharmas, the five faculties—eye and so forth—and the objects—visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)—are exclusively derived.
As for the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), it pertains to both types: earth, water, fire, and wind are the great elements, while the other seven [tangibles] are derived.

Tangible objects derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are those [tangibles] other than the [four] great elements themselves; the remaining sixty-four are not derived from the great elements. Regarding "truth" (*satya*) and "non-truth" (*asatya*):

"truth" refers to reality, namely suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). That which is contrary to these is called "non-truth. Seventy-three are truths.

Space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are non-truths because they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); therefore, they are not included within suffering, origin, or the path, and they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, they are not subsumed under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Regarding "appropriated" (*upātta*) and "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*):
those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are collectively grasped and maintained as a basis are called appropriated;

the opposite of this is called non-appropriated. Among the seventy-five dharmas, nine belong to both categories. The five sense organs, such as the eye, when abiding in the present, are called appropriated; [those] in the past...
Those of the future are called "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*). Those of the present that abide inseparable from the five sense faculties are called "appropriated" (*upātta*).

If they abide in the present and are not inseparable from the faculties, or those of the past and future, are called "non-appropriated. The remaining sixty-six [types of matter] are exclusively non-appropriated.
Regarding those with objects (*sālambana*) and those without objects (*anālambana*): the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are those that possess objects.
All phenomena that serve as conditions are objects of cognition; having such an object is called "having an object" (*sālambana*).
That which is contrary to this is called "without an object" (*anālambana*). Among the seventy-five dharmas, forty-seven types—consisting of the mind and mental factors—are those with objects;
the remaining twenty-eight are called those without objects. Regarding "maturation" (*vipāka*) and "non-maturation": their essence is neutral (*avyākṛta*). From...
The ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) is so named because it produces a result of a different category that matures; that which is contrary to this is called non-ripening (avipāka).

Among the eleven types of matter, the five sense organs, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility belong to both categories [ripening and non-ripening]. Sound and non-informative matter (avijñapti) are non-ripening. The mind-king (citta-rāja) belongs to both categories.
Among the forty-six mental factors (caitta-dharma), ten are universal ground-factors (mahābhūmika): vitarka, vicāra, and middha.
These thirteen factors all pertain to both types [of acquisition]. The remaining thirty-three—excluding the non-concomitant factors (viprayukta-dharma)—are not of the nature of maturation (vipāka).

Among them, the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and the homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) pertain to both types; the signless (animitta), maturation, and life-faculty (jīvitendriya) are exclusively of the nature of maturation; the two attainments (samāpatti) and non-acquisition (aprāpti) are of two types; names, phrases, and syllables (nāma-pada-vyañjana) are not of the nature of maturation;
and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are not of the nature of maturation. Regarding "view" (dṛṣṭi) and "non-view": it refers to observation and inference.

The term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is applied according to its specific nature; that which is contrary to this is called "non-view. Among the seventy-five factors (*dharmas*), wisdom (*prajñā*) pertains to both types:

if it is mundane right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, it is a view; if it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and so forth, it is not a view.
The eye is exclusively a view; the remaining seventy-three are exclusively non-views. Regarding the accumulated (*saṃcita*) and the unaccumulated (*asaṃcita*), [the former] is... at the extreme.
That which is subtle is called "accumulated" (*saṃcita*); that which is contrary to this is called "non-accumulated.

Among the seventy-five dharmas, the five faculties and the five objects are called "accumulated" because they are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*). The remaining sixty-five are all "non-accumulated," as they are not composed of atoms.
Regarding that which can cut, that which is cut, that which cannot cut, and that which cannot be cut: [the former] refers to axes and the like, while [the latter] refers to...

Among the seventy-five dharmas such as "cutting wood" and so forth, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are both the agent and the object of cutting, because they constitute the axe and so forth, as well as the wood and so forth.
It should be understood that the remaining seventy-one are neither the agent nor the object of cutting;

likewise, that which can weigh and that which is weighed, that which can be weighed and that which cannot be weighed, and that which can burn and that which is burned are to be understood in the same way. Regarding the faculties (*indriya*) and non-faculties (*anindriya*), [the former] increases...
The aforementioned are called faculties (*indriya*); those contrary to these are called non-faculties. The faculties consist of twenty-two:

the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, vigor faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

Regarding the known faculty (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), among the seventy-five dharmas, these thirteen—the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, faith, diligence, resolve, and life—are faculties; the remaining sixty-two are not faculties.

One should know that the two faculties of male and female are simply portions of the body faculty, while the five—pleasure, pain, joy, grief, and equanimity—are subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*); the latter three [faculties] are as previously described.
This has as its essence nine factors: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, bliss, and equanimity. Regarding which have maturation (*vipāka*) and which lack maturation:
unwholesome states and wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava*) possess maturation; neutral states (*avyākṛta*) and untainted states (*anāsrava*) lack maturation.

Among the eleven types of matter, visible form and sound, as well as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), pertain to both [types]. Among the forty-six mental factors (*caitasika*), the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) also pertain to both types.

Among the two Great Unwholesome Ground Dharmas and the two Minor Affliction Ground Dharmas—namely anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), vexation (*pradāśa*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), and resentment (*upanāha*)—and among the Indeterminate [Dharmas], remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and hatred (*dveṣa*):
these eleven possess only maturation (*vipāka*). The remaining thirty-five are common to both types [maturation and non-maturation].

Among the fourteen dissociated (*viprayukta*) [Dharmas], the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are common to both types; the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) possess maturation, while the remaining seven types do not.
The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not results of maturation (*vipāka*).

Briefly stated, there are twenty types of threefold classifications: the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three realms (*tridhātu*), the three abandonments (*prahāṇa*), the three trainings (*śikṣā*), those with vitarka and vicāra and so forth, the three stages (*bhūmi*), the three types of karma (*karman*), the Three Jewels (*triratna*), the three Piṭakas, the three trainings in ethical discipline (*śīla*), and those with vitarka and vicāra.

The three concentrations of purity, the three concentrations of the sages (muni), the three purities, the three types of misconduct, the three types of sublime conduct, the three types of clear knowledge (vidyā), the three demonstrations (prātihārya), the three kinds of samādhi, and the three doors of liberation.
Regarding the three natures: first, the wholesome; second, the unwholesome; and third, the indeterminate. There are seven kinds of wholesome [factors]:

first, those acquired at birth; second, those from hearing; third, those from reflection; fourth, those from cultivation; fifth, those of training; sixth, those of non-training; and seventh, those of neither-training-nor-non-training.

There are six types of non-learner (aśaikṣa), seven types of ultimate (paramārtha), and seven types of intermediate. Among these, the first four are with outflows (sāsrava) and the latter three are without outflows (anāsrava).

Within the category of those with outflows, the first is acquired through birth (upapatti-labdha) and the latter three are acquired through application (prāyogika). Within the category of those without outflows, the first two are conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the last one is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).

Regarding the unwholesome (akuśala), there is only one type; regarding the indeterminate (avyākṛta), there are two: the obscured (nivṛta) and the unobscured (anivṛta). Within the unobscured indeterminate, there are six types.

First, maturation; second, deportment; third, craftsmanship; fourth, fruition; fifth, intrinsic nature—the first four of these, when not subsumed under the indeterminate, are all termed "intrinsic nature.
Sixth, the ultimate. Among these six, the first five are conditioned and the last one is unconditioned;

together with the previously mentioned obscured [indeterminate], there are seven types of wholesome. There are seven types of unwholesome, one type of indeterminate, and seven types of indeterminate in total.
There are fifteen categories that exhaustively encompass all that is taught in the various treatises; by means of these fifteen, the seventy-five dharmas are analyzed.
Among the eleven types of form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*) pertains to all three natures: wholesome bodily and vocal actions are wholesome; unwholesome bodily and vocal actions are unwholesome;
and unmanifested neutral bodily actions, as well as non-action-forms, are neutral. Non-action-form refers to neutral bodily action that is not itself an informative act.

Regarding these, the vocal karma and the non-karmic sound are among the wholesome sounds that arise through innate acquisition (*upapatti-lābhika*) and through hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-maya*), because they are all capable of producing bodily and vocal karma.

Among the neutral (*avyākṛta*) sounds, there are both obscured (*nivṛta*) and unobscured (*anivṛta*) types. "Obscured" refers to the obscured-neutral bodily and vocal karma produced by the cultivation-path abandonments (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the First Dhyāna.
Within the unobscured [neutral], the category of form (*rūpa*) includes that which is of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).

Regarding the nature of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and the result of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*): sound includes the natures of deportment, craftsmanship, and the result of supernormal power.

When one who has been born in the second dhyāna or above speaks in a casual manner, it is because the mind of deportment belonging to the first dhyāna arises and produces [sound]; thus, sound includes the nature of deportment.

As for the five sense faculties—sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—they are exclusively non-obscured (*anivṛta*). Among these, the five sense faculties include the nature of maturation (*vipāka-svabhāva*). If one were to say...

That which arises from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is ripening (*vipāka*). If it is nurtured (*aupacayika*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—which pertain to ripening, deportment (*airyāpathika*), and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*);
these are the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). If it is nurtured, the three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as well as external odor, flavor, and tangibility, constitute its intrinsic nature;
these are non-defined (*avyākṛta*) because they are not ripening, nor are they the fruit of deportment or craftsmanship.

Because it is subsumed [by the mind], non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is categorized as wholesome or unwholesome, but not neutral; this is because a neutral mind is weak and thus does not produce non-informative action.

Within the wholesome, it is further divided into that which is innate (*upapatti-lābhika*) and that which is produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-maya*). Among these, that which is produced by hearing and reflection is non-informative action associated with the distracted state (*vikṣipta-avijñapti*);

that which is produced by cultivation is non-informative action associated with meditative concentration (*samāhita-avijñapti*). Furthermore, that which is produced by those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is non-informative action associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-avijñapti*).

The unwholesome consists solely of the non-informative (*avijñapti*) of the distracted mind; among the fifteen [mental factors], it excludes the wholesome by way of ultimate nature (*paramārtha-kuśala*).
The neutral by way of ultimate nature (*paramārtha-avyākṛta*) pervades the remaining twelve; this may be understood through inference based on the meaning.

Among the forty-six mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*), the ten universal ground factors (*mahābhūmika*), vitarka, vicāra, and middha—these thirteen—pervade all three natures. If one considers the ten universal ground factors...

Among the wholesome [states], investigation (*vicāra*) occurs throughout those born of acquisition (*upapattilābhika*), as well as those resulting from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śrutamayī*, *cintāmayī*, *bhāvanāmayī*); it occurs among the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) states, including both the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the unobscured (*anivṛta*).

Within the unobscured indeterminate, it occurs throughout those that are maturation-born (*vipākaja*), those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those of supernormal power (*nairmāṇika*). Regarding sleep (*middha*), within the wholesome it occurs only as that which is acquired at birth;
because the mind is weak, it does not extend to those resulting from hearing and so forth. Within the indeterminate, it occurs throughout both the obscured and the unobscured. As for the obscured:

In the desire realm, the non-obscured [states] associated with the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) pertain to both the maturation (*vipāka*), the deportment (*airyāpathika*), and the craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*);

they do not pertain to the fruit of mastery (*abhijñā-phala*) nor to the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*). The ten great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-kuśala*) are exclusively wholesome; among these, they include those acquired through birth (*upapatti-labdha*) as well as those resulting from hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā-maya*), and those pertaining to the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*).

The six great afflictive mental factors (*mahākleśabhūmika*) pertain to both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); if they are associated with the unwholesome, they are unwholesome.

These are unwholesome (*akuśala*). If they are associated with the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm, as well as the various afflictions of the two higher realms, they constitute the "obscured-unwholesome universal mental factors" (*nivṛtākuśalamahābhūmika*).

Among the two minor afflictions (*upakleśa*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), avarice (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), vexation (*pradāsa*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), and resentment (*upanāha*), as well as among the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), hatred (*dveṣa*)—these ten are exclusively unwholesome.

The three of guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*), along with greed (*lobha*), conceit (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—these six may be either [unwholesome or obscured-indeterminate].
Wholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is either unwholesome if it belongs to the desire realm, or obscured (*nivṛta*) if it belongs to the higher realms.

Because it is associated with mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; thus, it does not extend to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). When remorse arises regarding deportment (*īryāpatha*) or crafts (*śilpa*), it is merely a form of reflective examination (*pratyavekṣā*) and not [the type of] remorse [associated with wrongdoing].
Wholesome [remorse] is acquired only through birth (*upapatti-labdha*). Among the fourteen dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*), four are acquired.

Regarding the mutual inclusion of the three natures: within the wholesome, there are those acquired at birth, those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the learned (*śaikṣa*) and the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*). Within the neutral (*avyākṛta*), there are those that are obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and those that are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Within the unobscured-neutral, there are those that are maturation-born (*vipākaja*), those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those that are result-of-action (*nairmāṇika*).

Regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*) are exclusively wholesome; this refers to the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because they are originated by wholesome cultivation. Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*) are not included.

The matured life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) are exclusively non-obscured (*anivṛta*); among these, that which is not designated as "name," "phrase," or "syllable" is exclusively the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*).
The matured life-faculty and the non-conceptual attainment (*āsaṃjñika-samāpatti*) are exclusively maturation (*vipāka*).

Among the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is ultimately wholesome (*paramārtha-kuśala*), because it is both wholesome and permanent. Space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are [neither wholesome nor unwholesome].
The meaning is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Regarding the three realms: first, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); second, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and third, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

That which is bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm is called "belonging to the desire realm"; it should be known that the same applies to the form and formless realms. Among the eleven types of form, the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), visible form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) pertain to both the desire and form realms.
Fragrance (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*) belong only to the desire realm, because they are exclusively of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); therefore, they exist in the desire realm.

Because the body of sentient beings requires substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), this [scent and taste] exists only in the Desire Realm; since sentient beings in the higher realms do not require substantial food, these two do not extend to those realms.

Unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) extends across the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, and that which is unconditioned by either. If it is unmanifest form occurring in a non-concentrated state, it is bound to the Desire Realm;

if it is unmanifest form concomitant with meditative concentration, it belongs to the Form Realm; and if it is unmanifest form concomitant with the Path, it is unconditioned by either realm. Regarding form:

Within the realm [of form], there is no non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) that is dissociated [from thought], because that distracted mind is weak and can only produce informative [matter] (*vijñapti*), but cannot produce non-informative matter.
Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no non-informative matter, because there is no physical form (*rūpa*). Therefore, these eleven [bases] do not extend to the formless realm.

The five sense faculties and the five objects are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*); thus, they do not extend to the unconditioned (*anāsrava*). The mind-king (*cittarāja*) extends to all three realms as well as the unconditioned.

Among the forty-six mental factors (*caitta*), the ten universal factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the ten great wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) pertain to all three realms as well as the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are bound to the three realms, while those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are unconditioned.

The six great afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*) and, among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), *mada* (pride-intoxication), as well as greed (*rāga*), conceit (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) from the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), pertain to the bonds of the three realms. The two great unwholesome factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*) [pertain to the desire realm].

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), vexation (*pradāsa*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), and resentment (*upanāha*); and among the indeterminate [afflictions], hatred (*pratigha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), and sleep (*middha*)—these twelve exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The first ten are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) and therefore do not extend to the higher realms. Regret is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*), and since mental distress exists only in the desire realm, it does not extend to the higher realms.
Furthermore, because there is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the desire realm, sleep exists there; however, it does not exist in the higher realms.
Because there is no solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), there is no sleep; because [these states] are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are not unconditioned by the fetters.
Among the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*), the two factors of guile (*māyā*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*) pertain to both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Within the form realm, these two—guile and deceit—exist only in the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), because the Great Brahmā King, while dwelling among his own retinue of Brahmās, was suddenly subjected to interrogation and challenge by the Bhikṣu Aśvajit, and thus became deluded by guile and deceit.
The Brahmakāyika gods offer flattering words and express regretful apologies to Aśvajit for having stopped him on the mountain; therefore, there are both flattery (*māyā*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*).

In the two higher dhyānas, there is no reliance upon a multitude of others, as is the case in the first dhyāna; thus, flattery and deceit do not exist there. Within the stage of non-concentration (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), the two factors of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) pervade the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Within the form realm, applied thought extends up to the first dhyāna, while sustained thought also extends to the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).

Because one gradually becomes free from calamities and afflictions in the higher stages, there is no *vitarka* or *vicāra*. Among the fourteen dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain to all three realms (*dhātu-bandhana*) as well as to those that are non-bound (*abandhana*).

As for the *prāpti*, it pertains to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*)—which is bound to the three realms—and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), which is non-bound. The *asamanvāgama-prāpti*, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) pertain to all three realms.

Regarding names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), if they are said to follow speech, they are bound to two stages; in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are bound to that realm.
Regarding the first dhyāna, if one says it is bound to the five levels that follow the body—namely, the desire realm and the four dhyānas—that is correct;

however, even with these two explanations, both are consistent with the fact that the maturation (*vipāka*) of the desire realm, the form realm, and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*), as well as the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), exist only in the fourth dhyāna of the form realm.
This is because all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that only the maturation of the non-percipient state in the fourth dhyāna is true *nirvāṇa*.

Because one cultivates the cause of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in order to seek its fruit, which is the state of non-conception, it exists only in the fourth dhyāna and not in other stages.

The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) exists only in the formless realm and specifically at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); because this attainment of cessation involves the most subtle mental states and mental factors, it exists only at the Peak of Existence and not in the lower stages.
The three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are not bound to the three realms, as they are untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the three types of abandonment: first, abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*); second, abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); and third, that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

The eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), along with their associated and co-existent factors, are called "abandonable by seeing" because they are abandoned through the vision of the truths. The remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are "abandonable by cultivation" because they can only be abandoned through repeated practice.
Those whose nature is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and are thus neither abandonable by seeing nor by cultivation are called "not to be abandoned. [This applies to] form (*rūpa*).

Among the eleven [mental factors], non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is common to both that which is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and that which is not abandoned (*aheya*), as it pertains to both the distracted and the concentrated states; it is abandoned by cultivation when associated with the path, and is not abandoned when associated with the [uncontaminated] path.

As for the remaining ten [mental factors], they are abandoned only by cultivation. Among the forty-six mental concomitants (*caitasika*), the ten universal ground-dharmas (*mahābhūmika*) and the two—vitarka and vicāra—are common to all three types of abandonment.

The ten great wholesome ground-dharmas (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) are common to both being abandoned by cultivation and not being abandoned. The great afflictive ground-dharmas (*kleśamahābhūmika*)... [are abandoned only by cultivation].

The universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) are six; the unwholesome universal factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*) are two. Among the two indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), drowsiness (*middha*), greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*) are common to both abandonment by insight (*darśana-heya*) and abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
doubt (*vicikitsā*) is abandoned only by insight. The ten minor affliction universal factors (*parīttakleśa-mahābhūmika*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) are abandoned only by cultivation.

Among the fourteen dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), acquisition (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are common to all three types of abandonment; the remaining nine kinds are abandoned only by cultivation. The three unconditioned factors (*asaṃskṛta*) are not [subject to] abandonment at all.
[The category of] "abandoned" [is as follows]: Regarding the three types of learners—first, those in training (*śaikṣa*); second, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);

and third, those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)—the conditioned, untainted (*anāsrava*) states within the person in training are called "training" because they are still to be cultivated and practiced.

The conditioned, untainted states within the person beyond training are called "beyond training" because they have already reached fulfillment. All tainted (*sāsrava*) states and the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states are not objects of cultivation.
Because it is a dharma, it is not called "training" (*śaikṣa*), yet because it is not non-training (*aśaikṣa*)—since it is already fulfilled—it is not called "non-training.
Therefore, it is called "neither training nor non-training. Although the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) is also training, it is not called "training" because it is not ultimate.

Among the eleven types of form, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is common to all three trainings; the unmanifest that is co-existent with the path is training or non-training, while that which is co-existent with the path or is mundane (*vyutthita*) is only...

Those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa) comprise the remaining ten [mental factors], which are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner. The mind-kings (citta-rāja) pertain to all three types of training (traiśikṣa).

Among the forty-six mental concomitants (caitta-dharma), the ten universal ground-factors (mahābhūmika), the ten great wholesome ground-factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika), and vitarka and vicāra pertain to all three types of training;

the remaining twenty-four pertain exclusively to the neither-learner-nor-non-learner state. Among the fourteen dissociated factors (viprayukta-saṃskāra), four—namely, acquisition (prāpti) and the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa)—pertain to all three types of training.
Of the three trainings, the remaining nine types are exclusively neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee; the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are exclusively neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Regarding the three stages of "with vitarka and vicāra" and so forth: first, the stage with vitarka and vicāra refers to the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
second, the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra refers to the intermediate dhyāna; third, the stage without vitarka and without vicāra refers to the [second dhyāna] and above.
Regarding the stages above the dhyānas, because the dharmas arising based on the three [lower] stages differ, they are divided into three distinct categories.
Among the eleven types of matter (*rūpa*), odor (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*) exist only in the stage with vitarka and vicāra; the remaining nine types of matter pertain to all three stages.

Among the forty-six mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) associated with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the two categories—the unwholesome ground-dharmas (*akuśala-bhūmika*) and the minor affliction ground-dharmas (*parīttakleśabhūmika*)—include anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and envy (*īrṣyā*).

Among the indeterminate [factors], the thirteen—namely, vexation (*āghāta*), harm (*vihiṃsā*), resentment (*upanāha*), discursive thought (*vitarka*), sleep (*middha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), and anger (*krodha*)—exist only in the stage characterized by both discursive thought and sustained thought (*savitarkasavicārā bhūmi*).

Flattery (*māyā*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*), as well as sustained thought (*vicāra*), pertain to both the stage with both discursive and sustained thought and the stage with no discursive thought but only sustained thought (*avitarkavicāramātrā bhūmi*).

The remaining thirty factors pertain to all three stages. Among the dissociated [formations] (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain to all three stages.

The maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) belong exclusively to the stage that is without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra*). As for names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*):

if they are said to follow speech, they pertain to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), the First Dhyāna (*prathama-dhyāna*), which includes the stages with both applied and sustained thought (*savitarkasavicāra*), and the stage with no applied thought but only sustained thought (*avitarkavicāramātra*).

If they are said to follow the body, they pertain to all three realms. Regarding the three types of action (*karman*): first, bodily action (*kāyakarman*); second, vocal action (*vākkarman*); and third, mental action (*manaskarman*). That which is formative is called action (*karma*).
Because karma arises based on the body, it is called bodily karma; its nature consists of informative and non-informative [karma]. Because speech is designated as karma, it is called vocal karma;
its nature consists of informative and non-informative [karma]. Because it is originated by the mind, it is called mental karma; its essence is volition (*cetanā*).

Bodily informative [karma] has the ten material bases as its nature; vocal informative [karma] has sound as its nature; and both bodily and vocal non-informative [karma] have non-informative [matter] as their nature. Mental karma is volition itself.

It has volition (*cetanā*) as its nature among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). Regarding the Three Jewels: first, the Jewel of the Buddha; second, the Jewel of the Dharma; and third, the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

Because they are highly esteemed by the world, they are called "jewels" (*ratna*). Awakening is termed "Buddha"; it takes the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-pañca-skandha*) within the Buddha-body as its essence.
"Dharma" means that which guides and sustains (*naya-dhāraṇa*), namely Nirvāṇa; because it is virtuous, eternal, and most excellent, it is called the "Jewel of the Dharma."

The Sangha is defined as the harmonious assembly; it consists of the four paths and four fruits within the bodies of śrāvakas, comprising the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*), seventy-five dharmas—including non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the mental king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), the two [types of] investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*), the four attainments (*prāpti*), the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and the Buddha-Sangha Jewel—and pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha (cessation through discernment), which is exclusively a dharma.

The first is the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), which refers to untainted ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*); the second is the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), which refers to untainted concentration; and the third is the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), which refers to untainted wisdom.

Because they consist of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom, they are called "trainings. Regarding their nature: ethical discipline, among the eleven categories of form, has non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) as its nature;
