its nature consists of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) karma. "Vow concomitant with meditative concentration" (*dhyāna-samvara*) refers to that which exists simultaneously with meditative concentration;

its nature is impure (*sāsrava*) non-informative karma. "Vow concomitant with the path" (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) refers to that which exists simultaneously with the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*); it consists of untainted non-informative karma.

Regarding their intrinsic natures: among the seventy-five dharmas, the two types of informative intimation (*vijñapti*)—bodily and vocal—take the eleven types of form (*rūpa*) as their nature, specifically form and sound.
The three types of non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*) all take non-informative intimation itself as their nature.

Regarding the three meditative absorptions (dhyāna) characterized by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), first, the absorption with both applied and sustained thought refers to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna; second, the absorption without applied thought but with sustained thought refers to the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*); third...

The concentration without vitarka and without vicāra refers to the two concentrations from the second dhyāna upward; these all encompass both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) concentrations.

These three types all take concentration from among the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) as their essential nature, and they are divided into three kinds based on the differences in their associated states and levels.
Regarding the three types of pure concentration and so forth: "single-flavor concentration" refers to concentration associated with craving for the form and formless realms.

The two types of pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) refer to contaminated wholesome concentration; the three types of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) refer to concentration associated with untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).

All three of these have concentration among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) as their essential nature. Regarding the three forms of sagehood (*mauneya*): first, physical sagehood refers to the bodily karma of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
second, verbal sagehood refers to the vocal karma of one beyond training; third, mental sagehood refers to the... [mental karma of one beyond training].
The "Muni" of mental action (*manas-karma*) refers to one who is silent; because all afflictions and speech are silenced, he is a Muni.
The "Muni" of body and speech has the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) among the eleven material factors as its nature, while the "Muni" of mind has the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as its nature;
both are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the three purities: first, purity of body; second, purity of speech; third, purity of mind—these are temporary.
Because it is forever free from the stains of all unwholesome conduct and afflictions, it is called the "pure essential nature.
Its inclusion [within the categories] is as explained in the following section on the three types of sublime conduct (*sucarita*). The three types of unwholesome conduct (*duścarita*) are:

first, unwholesome physical conduct, which refers to all unwholesome bodily actions; second, unwholesome verbal conduct, which refers to all unwholesome vocal actions; and third, unwholesome mental conduct, which refers to all...
Unwholesome mental karma and that which is not mental karma—namely, greed, hatred, and wrong view—are called "misconduct" because these actions are evil.
Thus, bodily misconduct has as its nature the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) among the eleven categories of form; verbal misconduct has as its nature sound and the unmanifest;
and mental misconduct has as its nature volition (*cetanā*), greed, hatred, and wisdom among the mental factors (*caitta*). As for the three types of sublime conduct:

The three types of excellent conduct (*sucarita*) are as follows: first, excellent bodily conduct, which refers to all wholesome bodily karma; second, excellent verbal conduct, which refers to all wholesome verbal karma;
and third, excellent mental conduct, which refers to all wholesome mental karma, as well as non-mental karma consisting of non-greed, non-hatred, and right view.

Because these actions are themselves excellent, they are called "excellent conduct. Excellent bodily conduct consists of the [first] eleven categories of form (*rūpa*), namely, visible matter and unmanifest matter (*avijñapti*).
Vocal virtuous conduct has sound and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) as its nature; mental virtuous conduct has the mind’s intention—namely, non-attachment, non-hatred, and wisdom—as its nature.

Regarding the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): first, the clear knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānasākṣātkriyā-vidyā*), which remedies ignorance regarding the past, is the supernormal power of the realization of the recollection of past lives among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Second, the clear knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyā-vidyā*) remedies ignorance regarding the future.

Ignorance regarding the middle [time] is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) among the six supernormal powers. Regarding the treatment of ignorance concerning the three times: ignorance regarding the past is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*); ignorance regarding the future is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).

As for the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows among the six supernormal powers, it consists of two types of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and one of each of the following:

the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). If these take the exhaustion of outflows as their object, they are of the nature of six knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*). If they arise within the continuum of one who has exhausted the outflows, then...
Regarding the nature of the ten knowledges, these three all have wisdom (*prajñā*) among the mental factors as their essential nature. As for the three demonstrations (*prātihārya*):

first, the demonstration of miraculous power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣaya-abhijñā*) among the six supernormal powers; its nature is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Second, the demonstration of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*) is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) among the six supernormal powers;

its nature consists of five knowledges, namely: dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

The three mental instructions and guidances (*manopavicāra*) are either the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) among the six supernormal powers, or they consist of six knowledges or ten knowledges as previously explained.

Because they can demonstrate and guide, they receive the name "instruction and guidance. These three all have wisdom (*prajñā*) among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) as their essential nature.
As for the three kinds of samādhi: first, the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), which refers to [the contemplation of] emptiness and non-self.
The two signless samādhis associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) refer to the meditative concentrations associated with the four aspects of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The Truth of Cessation is "signless" because it is devoid of the ten signs—namely, the five [objects] such as form, male and female, the two [perceptions], and the three conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
The meditative concentration that takes this as its object receives the name "signless. The three wishless (*apraṇihita*) samādhis take suffering as their object.
The concentration associated with the ten aspects of the truth of the origin (*samudaya*) is called "the tenfold" because it consists of:

impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), cause (*hetu*), origin (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), condition (*pratyaya*), path (*mārga*), right method (*nyāya*), practice (*pratipad*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*). The two truths of suffering and origin are to be reviled; the path is like a raft that must necessarily be abandoned.

Because the meditative absorption that takes these as its object attains the name "wishless" (*apraṇihita*), the aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*) and non-self (*anātman*) are not to be reviled or abandoned, as they are [inseparable from the nature of phenomena].
Because their characteristics are similar to those of *nirvāṇa*, these three are not associated [with it].

Among all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), these three are definitively established as having concentration (*samādhi*) as their essential nature. Regarding the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*): first, the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*);
second, the gate of wishlessness (*apranihita-vimokṣamukha*); and third, the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). One should know that these serve as the entrance gates to *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*) states within the first three meditative concentrations (*samādhi*),

there are briefly twenty-two types when analyzed according to four categories: the four truths, the four nutriments (*āhāra*), the four bodily fetters (*kāyabandhana*), the four perversions (*viparyāsa*),

the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the four conditions (*pratyaya*), the four modes of birth (*yoni*), the four types of karma (*karman*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the four wholesome [roots].

The faculties, the four paths, the four fruits, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the four immeasurables, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four paths of practice, the four paths, and the four kinds of verified confidence.
Regarding the Four Truths: first, the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), which refers to the nature of affliction within the results of outflows (*āsrava*);

second, the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), which refers to that which can summon and accumulate [suffering], namely the causes of outflows; third, the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*)... [arising].

Because death is severed, it is called cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Because it has the sense of being traversed by the four noble truths and the paths, it is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

Among the seventy-five dharmas, twenty-nine—namely, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the king of the mind (the mind itself), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*mahākuśala-bhūmika*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), vitarka and vicāra, acquisition (*prāpti*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—pertain to all three truths:
suffering, origin, and the path. Cessation through deliberation pertains solely to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The remaining forty pertain to all [four] truths.

Among the five [unconditioned phenomena], excluding space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the remaining forty-three are included within both the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*).
Space and non-analytical cessation are not subsumed under the four truths, as explained previously. Regarding the four nutriments (*āhāra*): first, edible food; second, contact-food;

third, volition-food; and fourth, consciousness-food. They are called "nutriments" because they provide sustenance and benefit. All of these are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*). Among the eleven categories of form, those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)...

Fragrance, flavor, and tangibility are called the food of mouthfuls (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*), contact (*sparśa*) is called the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*); volition (*cetanā*) is called the food of volition (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*); and the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is called the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

Regarding the four bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*): first, the bodily fetter of sensual desire (*abhidhyākāyagrantha*); second, the bodily fetter of ill-will (*vyāpādakāyagrantha*); third, the bodily fetter of attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśakāyagrantha*);

and fourth, the bodily fetter of dogmatic adherence to "this alone is the truth" (*tattvābhiniveśakāyagrantha*). The five categories of craving belonging to the desire realm are termed the first bodily fetter.

The category of hatred (*pratigha*) is called the second *kāyabandhana* (bodily bond). The six types of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) constitute the third *kāyabandhana*.

The twelve types of views (*dṛṣṭi*) constitute the fourth *kāyabandhana*. They are called "bodily bonds" (*kāyabandhana*) because they variously bind the physical basis (*ātmabhāva*) of sentient beings; they carry the meaning of a snare that ensnares the bodies of sentient beings.

The first two have greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*pratigha*) from among the indeterminate factors as their essence, while the latter two have the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as their essence.
The essence consists of middle-level wisdom. Regarding the four perversions: first, the perversion of grasping at the impermanent as permanent;
second, the perversion of grasping at suffering as pleasure; third, the perversion of grasping at the impure as pure; and fourth, the perversion of grasping at the non-self as self.
The first of these has the view of eternalism within the view of extremes as its essence; the latter two have the estimation of pleasure and purity within the clinging to views as their essence.
Regarding their essential nature, the last one [the view of self] has the view of self within the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its essence;

some say that the inversion of self subsumes the entirety of the view of a personal identity, and all of these have wisdom (*prajñā*) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as their intrinsic nature. As for the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), they are: first, the station of consciousness in form; second, the station of consciousness in feeling;

third, the station of consciousness in perception; and fourth, the station of consciousness in formations. Because consciousness becomes attached to them, they are called "stations of consciousness"; they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).

The four aggregates consist only of those included within the category of sentient beings; among the seventy-five dharmas, excluding the mind-king (citta-rāja) and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), the remainder are designated as the four stations of consciousness (vijñāna-sthiti) as appropriate.

Regarding the four dhyānas—namely, the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas—they are called "dhyāna" because, through the tranquility of meditative concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā) is able to deliberate with precision. Among the seventy-five dharmas...

The five faculties beginning with the eye; visible form, sound, and tangible objects; non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); the mind-king (*citta-rāja*); the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*);
the ten afflictive universal factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*); the six types of pride (*māna*), greed (*lobha*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*);

acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*); the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); the four dhyānas; guile (*māyā*) and deceit (*śāṭhya*); vitarka and vicāra—these exist only in the first dhyāna; and names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), if one speaks of them...
According to the [specific] teaching, it belongs only to the first dhyāna; however, if explained in terms of the body, it extends through all four dhyānas.

The fruition of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the meditative attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) belong only to the fourth dhyāna. Regarding the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), they are:

(1) the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), (2) the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), (3) the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and (4) the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Among these four, the first three arise from preparatory effort (*prayoga*).

Regarding the establishment of these names: in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one contemplates infinite space and is able to easily dissociate from form; thus it is named the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Having contemplated that space, one next contemplates the consciousness that takes it as its object, forming the understanding that consciousness is infinite; thus it is named the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Next, one contemplates that the consciousness which takes [space] as its object is non-existent; thus it is named the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). The final [sphere] is named according to its essential nature.

The name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā) is established because it is not that there is coarse perception (*saṃjñā*), nor is it that there is no perception at all; rather, it means there is a subtle and feeble perception.

It is called the "Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) because it is not the same as the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) where mental factors and perceptions are entirely absent; it is the place where sentient beings are born and grow.

Because it is formless (*arūpa*), it is given the name "Formless. Among the seventy-five dharmas, these include the mind-king (*cittarāja*), the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), and the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika-dharma*).

The ten universal defiled mental factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*) are: the six—conceit (*māna*), greed (*lobha*), pride (*mada*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*);

the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). These exist exclusively in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Regarding the four conditions (*pratyaya*): first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which means that causes themselves are conditions;

this refers to the nature of the five causes, excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Second, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), where "immediately preceding" (*samantara*) means "equal" (*sama*).

1. The immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is synonymous with the "equal-and-immediate" condition; its nature consists of all previously arisen mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), excluding the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat.
2. The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is synonymous with the "object" condition; its nature consists of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*). 3.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is synonymous with the "dominant" condition; it is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), and its nature likewise consists of all phenomena.

Regarding their nature, if one excludes the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas from the seventy-five dharmas based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they pervade the remaining seventy-two dharmas.

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) pervades the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and the forty-six mental concomitants (*caitta*). The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) pervade all seventy-five dharmas.
As for the four modes of birth (*yoni*): first, viviparous; second, oviparous; third, moisture-born; and fourth, transformation-born.

The nature of birth as a maturation (*vipāka*) consists of the five aggregates. Among the seventy-five dharmas, these include: the five faculties of the eye and so forth; visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects; the mind-king; the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*);
vitarka, vicāra, sleep, acquisition (*prāpti*), and the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*); the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); and the four characteristics.

Regarding the four modes of birth, the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñisamāpatti-vipāka*) occurs only through miraculous birth (*upapāduka*). As for the four types of karma: first, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*), which refers to [karma] in this very existence.
1. Karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya-karma*): This refers to karma created in this life that ripens in the second life. 2.

Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariya-vedanīya-karma*): This refers to karma created in this life that ripens sequentially from the third life onward. 3. Karma to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyata-vedanīya-karma*):

Because it is not fixed as to when it will be experienced, it is designated by the name "indeterminate. All of these are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and pertain to both the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Among the seventy-five wholesome dharmas, matter (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)—as well as volition (*cetanā*) among the mental factors (*caitta*)—are all of the nature of karma and thus pertain to all four types of karma.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): first, the foundation of mindfulness of the body; second, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; third, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and fourth, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma*).

These take wisdom (*prajñā*) from among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as their essential nature, while the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena serve as their respective objects of observation (*ālambana*).

Wisdom is designated as "application of mindfulness to the body" (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, based on its object and its associates. Regarding the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*):

first, warmth (*uṣmagata*); second, summits (*mūrdhan*); third, patience (*kṣānti*); and fourth, the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). That which is called "warmth" is the precursor to the fire of the noble paths;

it is called "summit" because it is like a mountain peak, being at the boundary between advancing and retreating. It is called "patience" because the mind is able to endure the principles of the Four Noble Truths. There is... [text continues].

Because they are subject to outflows (*āsrava*), they are called "mundane" (*laukika*); because they are superior to [the mundane] heat (*uṣmagata*) and the other [stages], they are called "supreme" (*agra*).

Both have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence. They are associated with and coexist with the five aggregates (*skandha*) as their nature. Among the seventy-five dharmas, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), the two—vitarka and vicāra—and the four characteristics of acquisition (*prāpti-lakṣaṇa*) all pertain to these four types.
Regarding the four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*): first, the stage of approaching stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*); second, [the stage of approaching once-returning].

The candidates for the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), Non-returner (anāgāmin), and Arhat (arhat)—each according to their respective application—take the untainted five aggregates as their nature.

Because they are directed toward the fruits, they are called "candidates" (*pratipannaka*). Among the seventy-five dharmas, the unmanifest form (*avijñapti*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), the ten [wholesome] factors such as investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) all pertain to the four candidates. The four fruits are as follows: [the fruit of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arhat].

There are four fruits: first, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*); second, the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*); third, the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*); and fourth, the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*). Regarding the fruit of stream-entry:
the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is collectively termed "stream" (*srotas*), because by means of this as a cause, one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*.

The term "entry" (*pre*) is used to indicate that one has for the first time attained that stream; thus, it is called "stream-entry. As for the "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*): such a person goes to the heavenly realms.
One who returns once more to the human realm and there attains parinirvāṇa is therefore called the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

One who does not return to be born again in the desire realm is therefore called a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*). An Arhat—here translated as "The Worthy One" (*arhan*)—is so called because they are solely worthy of transforming others;
because they are worthy of being venerated by all sentient beings, they are called "Worthy. Because they have attained what was sought and achieved, they are called [Arhats].
The fruits, according to their respective applications, all have as their nature the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Among the seventy-five dharmas, unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten [mental factors] of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*), acquisition (*prāpti*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the unconditioned phenomenon of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskrta*) all pertain to the four fruits.
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): first, the fearlessness of being perfectly awakened, [expressed as]: "In regard to me..."

All phenomena are perfectly awakened; because one has no fear when encountering external challenges, the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) constitute its nature. Regarding the fearlessness concerning the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*):
"I have attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows," because one has no fear when encountering external challenges, it either has six knowledges or ten knowledges as its nature.
If the exhaustion of outflows is taken as the object, it has six knowledges as its nature—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

The conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) regarding the exhaustion of birth and cessation consists of ten knowledges (*jñāna*) when acquired within the body of one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*). Regarding the first [fearlessness], the fearlessness concerning the obstructive dharmas:

"I have taught my disciples the dharmas that constitute obstructions; for those who are defiled, these will certainly act as obstructions. This is because there is no dread even when encountering external challenges.

It has eight knowledges as its nature, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). Regarding the second [fearlessness], the fearlessness concerning the path leading out: "I have taught my disciples... [the path leading out]. It has four knowledges as its nature.
