fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from intoxicants. Of these, the first three and the last one are bodily actions; the fourth is [verbal action].
Regarding the nature of vocal and bodily karma—both manifest and unmanifest: bodily manifest action has as its nature "form" (rūpa) among the eleven categories of form;
vocal manifest action has as its nature "sound" (śabda); and both bodily and vocal unmanifest action have as their nature "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
As for the five eyes: first, the fleshly eye; second, the divine eye; third, the wisdom eye; fourth, the Dharma eye; and fifth, the Buddha eye. The fleshly eye refers to that of the desire realm...

The "sentient-being eye" and the "divine eye" refer to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The "wisdom eye" (*prajñācakṣus*) and the "dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*) have wisdom as their essence;
observing the principle of the Four Noble Truths is called the wisdom eye, while establishing the knowledge of phenomena (*vastujñāna*) is called the dharma-eye.

As for the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*), these aforementioned four eyes, when present within the body of a Buddha, are collectively termed the Buddha-eye; among the seventy-five dharmas, its nature consists of the eye and wisdom.
The first two are exclusively the eye; the next two are exclusively wisdom; and the last one pertains to both the eye and the observation and inference of wisdom.
Accordingly, they are named "eye.
There are five general types of sixfold distinctions: the six elements, the six supernormal powers, the six impurities, the six causes, and the six perfections.
The six elements (dhātu) are: first, earth; second, water; third, fire; fourth, wind; fifth, space; and sixth, consciousness. In terms of their essential nature, they are called "elements.

The first four are the four great elements (mahābhūta) within the category of tangible objects (spraṣṭavya). Space is the space element (ākāśadhātu). Form is subsumed under the category of form (rūpa), specifically consisting of shadows, light, darkness, and luster.

Consciousness is the mind-king (cittarāja), which is exclusively with outflows (sāsrava). Regarding the six supernormal powers (abhijñā): the first is the knowledge of the power of psychic transformation (ṛddhiviṣaya-jñāna).

The supernormal power of realization (*abhijñā*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), its object (*ālambana*), and the wisdom of transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-jñāna*). Because there is no obstruction when realizing these objects, it is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*). It is named after both the meditative absorption and the object that serves as the means of realization.

Although other supernormal powers also rely upon meditative concentration, this one’s characteristics are most prominent; thus, it is specifically designated by the name "supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*).

Regarding the supernormal power of divine sight (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), the divine eye is the supporting faculty (*indriya*), while the wisdom is the discernment associated with visual consciousness.

When wisdom realizes its object without obstruction, it is called a "penetration" (*abhijñā*); this name is derived from both the faculty and the realizing agent. Third, regarding the penetration of the divine ear:

when the wisdom that realizes the divine ear—this being the faculty, while the wisdom is the discernment associated with the ear-consciousness—realizes its object without obstruction, it is called a penetration;

this name is likewise derived from both the faculty and the realizing agent. Fourth, regarding the penetration of the knowledge of others' minds: the penetration that realizes [others' minds] is named according to its preparatory application (*prayoga*) and...

1. The supernormal power of the realization of the divine ear (*dibbasota-ñāṇa-abhiññā*) is named after the faculty that realizes it. 2. The supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa-abhiññā*) is named after the object, the associated states, and the realizing faculty. 3.

The supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa-abhiññā*) is named after the object, the associated states, and the realizing faculty. 4. Regarding the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa-abhiññā*):

if "destruction of the taints" refers to *nibbāna*, it is named after the realized state and the realizing knowledge; if "destruction of the taints" refers to the person whose taints are destroyed, it is named after the basis [the body] and the realizing knowledge.

Regarding the names [of the superknowledges], among the six *abhijñās*, the first four are comprised solely within conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). The knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-abhijñā*) is comprised of five knowledges, namely:

dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds. As for the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*), if it takes the exhaustion of outflows as its object, it consists of six knowledges in nature—excluding path-knowledge, suffering-knowledge, origin-knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds.
If it arises based on a body that has exhausted the outflows, it consists of ten knowledges in nature. All of these are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
Its essential nature is wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the six stains (*mala*): first, vexation; second, injury; third, resentment; fourth, guile; fifth, deception; and sixth, arrogance.

These six take the six factors from the "Basic Level of Minor Defilements" (*parīttakleśabhūmi*) as their nature; because they possess the characteristic of being defiled and coarse, they are called "stains.

The six causes (*hetu*) are: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*); second, the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*); third, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*); and fourth, the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).

Regarding the five universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the six maturation causes (*vipāka-hetu*), and the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*): that which can act as a cause for a fruit is called an "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

This may mean that the efficient action itself is the cause, or that the cause of the efficient action is the efficient cause; it takes all phenomena as its nature and pervades all seventy-five factors. Regarding the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*):
that which exists simultaneously with its fruit is called a "co-existent cause. This may mean that co-existence itself is the cause, or...

The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is named as such because it exists simultaneously; its substance consists of seventy-two dharmas across the three time periods, excluding the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas.

Regarding the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is called "similar-type" because cause and effect are similar; it is either the similar-type itself that is the cause, or the cause of the similar-type, hence it is named the similar-type cause.
Its substance consists of seventy-two dharmas of the past and present, excluding the three unconditioned dharmas.

Regarding the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*): the equality of five meanings is termed "association. Association itself is the cause, or the cause of association is termed the associated cause.
Its substance consists of the forty-six minds and mental factors across the three time periods. Regarding the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*):
it acts as a cause for all defiled phenomena of the five categories. Pervasiveness itself is the cause, thus it is named the pervasive cause; one must not say [otherwise].

Since universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) also serve as causes for non-universal phenomena, their substance consists of the eleven universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the past and present categories of suffering and origin,
along with their concomitant factors. Among the seventy-five dharmas, these include the mind-king (*citta*), the ten great ground-dharmas (*mahābhūmika*),
the ten great affliction-ground-dharmas (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the six unwholesome ground-dharmas (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), and the two— vitarka, vicāra, and middha.

Regarding the nature of the four characteristics of sleep and doubt as *vipāka-hetu* (maturation cause): "maturation cause" refers to that which is itself maturation and is the cause, or that which is the cause of maturation.
Its nature consists of the unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of the three time periods. It takes as its substance seventy-five dharmas:
form, sound, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the mind-king, forty-six mental factors (*caitta*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the four characteristics.

The six *pāramitās* are: first, generosity (*dāna*); second, pure ethical discipline (*śīla*); third, patience (*kṣānti*); fourth, diligence (*vīrya*); fifth, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and sixth, wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding "pāra" (the other shore), this refers to *nirvāṇa*. Because these six are called "honey" (*madhu*), being able to reach *nirvāṇa*, the further shore, they are called "reaching the further shore" (*pāramitā*).
As for generosity, it means being able to give away material wealth, the Dharma, and so forth. Because one is able...
Its nature consists of the volition (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) that initiate it, as well as the two types of action—bodily and vocal—that are initiated by them;

among the seventy-five dharmas, its nature comprises matter (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*), and applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) has the three types of restraint as its nature; among the eleven categories of matter, its nature consists of matter, sound, and non-informative matter. It is peaceful (*praśānta*).
The patience [of the bodhisattva] has as its nature the root of non-aversion among the great wholesome mental factors;
diligence has as its nature the vigor among the great wholesome mental factors; meditative concentration has as its nature the samādhi among the universal mental factors;
and wisdom has as its nature the prajñā among the universal mental factors.

The analysis according to the seven gates consists briefly of five types: the seven kinds of pride (*māna*), the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the seven kinds of noble persons (*āryapudgala*), the seven branches of morality (*śīlāṅga*), and the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Regarding the seven kinds of pride: (1) pride (*māna*), (2) excessive pride (*atimāna*), (3) pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), (4) the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), (5) overweening pride (*adhimāna*), (6) inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and (7) false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
If one considers oneself superior to those who are inferior, or equal to those who are equal...

The general definition of pride (*māna*) is that which causes the mind to become haughty. To consider oneself superior to those who are equal, or to consider oneself equal to those who are superior, such that the mind becomes haughty, is collectively termed "excessive pride" (*atimāna*).
To consider oneself superior to those who are actually superior, such that the mind becomes haughty, is termed "pride beyond pride" (*mānātimāna*).
To rely on the notion of "I" and cause the mind to become haughty is termed "the pride of self" (*asmimāna*). [If one considers oneself superior] to those who have not yet attained excellence...
Among the types of excellence, to think that one has attained what one has not and thereby cause the mind to become uplifted is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
To think that one is only slightly inferior when one is actually much inferior and thereby cause the mind to become uplifted is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).

To think that one possesses qualities when one lacks them and thereby cause the mind to become uplifted is called *mithyāmāna* (false pride), as its essence consists of pride within uncertainty. [Next are] the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

There are those with different bodies and different perceptions, such as humans and a portion of the gods; "a portion of the gods" refers to the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those of the first dhyāna, excluding those born at the beginning of the kalpa.
"Different bodies" means that their physical forms (*rūpakāya*) differ in various colors, shapes, and appearances.

"Different perceptions" means that they possess the distinctions between the perceptions of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Second, there are those with different bodies and one perception.
Just as the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm conceive such a notion at the beginning of a kalpa— that these various Brahmakāyika gods all arise from Great Brahmā—
and at that time Great Brahmā likewise conceives this notion that "all these Brahmakāyika gods are born from me"—

because they share the same notion of a single cause, he is called the "Great Brahmā of One Notion. As for the body of the Great Brahmā King, its dimensions are lofty and vast, and his countenance and majestic virtue are sublime.

Because each detail—such as speech, radiance, clothing, and headgear—is distinct from that of the Brahma assembly, it is called "difference of body" (*kāya-bheda*). Regarding "one perception" (*eka-saṃjñā*) and "difference of perception" (*nānā-saṃjñā*):

In the two meditative absorptions (the second and third dhyānas) and the three heavens [of those absorptions], their manifested forms and features are not different; therefore, it is called "oneness of body. In the first dhyāna, because there is a mixture of the perceptions of pleasure, non-pain-pleasure, and suffering, it is called "difference of perception.

In the fourth dhyāna, because there is one body and one perception, it is called "oneness of body and oneness of perception. (Note: The term *tri-dhyāna* in the source refers to the three heavens of the first three dhyānas; here, based on the context of the four dhyānas and the subsequent mention of the fourth, the text intends to contrast the first three with the fourth.)

The three heavens are designated as "one body" because their physical forms and appearances are not different; they are designated as "one perception" because they possess only the perception of pleasure.

Within the first dhyāna, it is said to have "one perception" due to the presence of defiled perception; in the second dhyāna, it is said to have "different perceptions" due to the presence of two types of wholesome perception;
and in the third dhyāna, it is said to have "one perception" due to the presence of ripened (vipāka) perception. [The fifth is] emptiness.
In the Sphere of Infinite Space, there are six consciousnesses; in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, seven; and in the Sphere of Nothingness, the remaining three.
Because the fourth dhyāna and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) both contain factors that destroy consciousness, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

These seven stations of consciousness consist only of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) five aggregates of the desire and form realms, or the four aggregates of the formless realm; among the seventy-five dharmas, the three unconditioned [dharmas] are excluded.

The nature [of these states] consists, as appropriate, of the ninety-two factors excluding the maturation of non-perception and the two meditative attainments. Regarding the seven types of noble persons: first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*);

second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth, the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); fifth, the bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*);

sixth, the one liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*); and seventh, the one doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). As for the "follower by faith," they are so called because in the preceding stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), they proceeded by following faith.

The Dharma-follower (dharmānusārī) is so called because they follow the Dharma during the preliminary stage (*prayoga-avasthā*). The one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) is so called because the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) has increased.

The one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is so called because the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) has increased. The body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*) is so called because they have personally realized the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with the body.

The one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) is so called because they are freed from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) solely through the power of wisdom. The one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) additionally attains the meditative attainment of cessation.

Because they have abandoned the obstacles to liberation, the first two are the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the next three are the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the final two are the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

These seven noble beings (*ārya-pudgala*) all take the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) as their nature. If one analyzes them according to the seventy-five dharmas, they consist of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*mahākuśala-bhūmika-dharma*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). (7)

The branch precepts (*śīla-aṅga*) are: first, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from harsh speech;

sixth, abstaining from divisive speech; and seventh, abstaining from frivolous speech. The first three are of the nature of bodily action (*kāya-karman*), consisting of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter.

The latter four are of the nature of vocal action (*vāk-karman*), consisting of both informative and non-informative matter. Regarding bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti*), it consists of the "matter" (*rūpa*) among the eleven types of matter.
The nature of vocal intimation is sound; the nature of non-intimation is non-intimation. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment: first, mindfulness; second, concentration;
third, investigation of phenomena; fourth, joy; fifth, pliancy; sixth, equanimity; and seventh, vigor.

The first four have as their essence mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and feeling from among the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika). The latter three have as their essence pliancy from among the great wholesome mental factors (kuśalamahābhūmika).
Equanimity has the nature of relinquishment; "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the meaning of being a factor of awakening-wisdom (*bodhyaṅga*).
There are five types of eightfold classifications: the Eight Precepts, the Eightfold Noble Path, the Eight Liberations, the Eight Bases of Mastery, and the Eight Difficulties.
Regarding the Eight Precepts: first, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech... [and so forth].
1. Refraining from false speech; 2. Refraining from drinking intoxicants; 3–6. Refraining from anointing with perfumes, wearing garlands, and engaging in singing, dancing, or watching performances;

7. Refraining from sleeping or sitting on high, broad, and luxurious beds or seats; 8. Refraining from eating at improper times. The first three and the last four are subsumed under bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

One does not go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or theatrical performances; therefore, these are subsumed under bodily action—or perhaps they are not [subsumed under] singing, dancing, and so forth.
This is subsumed under vocal action; the fourth [category] is subsumed under both bodily and vocal actions, possessing the nature of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*).

Bodily informative action has as its nature the "matter" among the eleven types of matter; vocal informative action has sound as its nature; and the non-informative aspects of body and speech have non-informative matter as their nature.
Among the ten precepts, the sixth is divided into two, with the addition of the prohibition against handling gold, silver, and precious objects.

It constitutes the tenth category: the informative and non-informative nature of bodily action (*kāyakarma-vijñapti-avijñapti*). As for the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*): first, right view; second, right mindfulness;
third, right concentration; fourth, right effort; fifth, right thought; sixth, right speech; seventh, right action; and eighth, right livelihood.

The first three have, respectively, wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*)—as found among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*)—as their intrinsic nature. Right effort has [right] application (*vīrya*) as its intrinsic nature, which belongs to the wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*).

Right effort has diligence as its nature; right thought has discursive investigation (*vitarka*) and analytical examination (*vicāra*) within the indeterminate as its nature; the three [factors]—speech, action, and livelihood—have the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) among the material as their nature;
all are untainted (*anāsrava*). As for the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*): first, possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms;
second, without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; third, the pure liberation; fourth, the sphere of infinite space; fifth...

1. The Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; 2. The Sphere of Nothingness; 3. The Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; 4. The Cessation of Feeling and Perception. Regarding the first liberation:

when one possesses the perception of form within the internal body and has a craving for that perception of form, one contemplates external impure forms, such as a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*), in order to eliminate that craving for perception.

By doing so, one causes craving not to arise with respect to the internal body; this is called the first liberation. [The second liberation] is when there is no perception of form within the internal body.
Although greed has already been eliminated, because greed remains stubbornly persistent, one contemplates external impurities such as the color of a livid corpse so that greed does not arise;
this is called the second liberation. Contemplating pure forms so that greed does not arise is called the "pure liberation.

Because the four formless attainments—beginning with the sphere of infinite space—manifest contemplation that is increasingly superior and each can liberate one from the greed of the lower stages, they follow next.

The fourth liberation is the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which involves turning away from sensation and so forth; this is called the eighth liberation, for the meaning of "turning away" (*parāṅmukha*) is the meaning of "liberation.
The first three liberations have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature, because they directly counteract attachment.

If their associated factors (*sānucara*) are included, they consist of all five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The next four liberations have the wholesome states of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as their nature. The final liberation has... [as its nature].

The nature of the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is as follows: if one defines its substance according to the seventy-five dharmas, the first two [liberations] have as their substance non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa), the mind-king (citta-rāja), the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma), vitarka and vicāra, and the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa). The third [liberation] excludes vitarka and vicāra;
the rest are as explained for the first two. The four formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa) have as their substance the mind-king and the ten universal mental factors.

The last liberation has the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as its essence; the first two rely on the first two dhyānas; the third relies on the fourth dhyāna; the next four each rely on their own respective stages;
and the last one relies on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). As for the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):

first, having the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are few; second, having the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms that are many; third, having no perception of internal forms...

One contemplates external forms as few while being without internal perception of form; one contemplates external forms as many while being without internal perception of form—these constitute four bases.
Then, contemplating external forms as blue, yellow, red, and white constitutes another four bases, making eight in total.

Because there is attachment to the perception of form within one's own internal body, one contemplates external forms as few, such as a bloated corpse (*vinīlaka*), as an antidote; this is called the first stage of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). Within one's own internal body, there is...
Taking the desire for perceptions of form as the object to be countered, one contemplates many external forms as bluish corpses and so forth; this is called the second stage of mastery.

Having no perception of form internally regarding one’s own body, but desiring to prevent the arising of desire by contemplating few external forms as bluish corpses and so forth for the sake of firm stability, this is called the third stage of mastery.
Having no perception of form internally regarding one’s own body, but desiring only... [the text continues].
Observing external forms as predominantly blue, such as a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth, so that desire does not arise, is called the fourth *abhibhvāyatana*.

Furthermore, while one has no perception of form internally regarding the body, yet desire remains, one merely exerts the mind or examines the afflictions by observing the four external colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—so that desire does not arise;
these are called the latter four *abhibhvāyatanas*. The essential nature and other characteristics of the first two *abhibhvāyatanas* are as previously described.

Because the first liberation (*vimokṣa*) is the fruit of the first liberation, the nature and basis of the next two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are like those of the second liberation, as they are the fruit of the second liberation.
Because the latter four spheres of mastery are like the third liberation, they are the fruit of the third liberation.
While the prior cultivation of the liberations involves only the relinquishing of what is behind, the subsequent cultivation of the spheres of mastery [involves both].

They are called "mastery objects" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because one is able to master the objects of perception, observing them according to one's will, or else because the mind does not arise at all toward those superior realms;
thus they are named "mastery. As for the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*): first, hell; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghost realm; fourth, Uttarakuru;

fifth, the heaven of non-conceptual beings; sixth, being possessed of worldly wit and eloquence; seventh, the period before a Buddha appears or after a Buddha has passed away; eighth, being blind, deaf, or mute, such that one cannot enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*).

Furthermore, because they are free from defilement, they are called "difficult. Worldly wisdom and eloquence have false wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*) as their nature among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
The remaining seven [faculties] all have the five aggregates (*skandha*)—which are maturation-born and indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*)—as their nature.

Among the seventy-five dharmas, the five faculties such as the eye, the five objects such as form, smell, taste, and touch, the mind-king, the ten universal mental factors, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), torpor (*middha*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) [are included].
The nature of these consists, as appropriate, of perception, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

There are five general categories for the ninefold classification: the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*), the nine stages (*bhūmi*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvasamāpatti*), and the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).

Regarding the nine fetters: first, the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*); second, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); third, the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*); fourth, the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).

The five fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the six fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), the seventh fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), the eighth fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), and the ninth fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*):

these nine fetters, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, collectively take one hundred matters as their nature. The fetters of craving (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) each consist of the five categories within the three realms, totaling forty-five matters.

The fetter of hostility (*pratigha*) exists only in the five categories of the desire realm, totaling five matters. The fetter of views consists of eighteen matters; namely, [the five views]... [there are]... [the remaining views].

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) each consist of six objects, being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) within each of the three realms.

False views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) consist of twelve objects, being four categories (*prakāra*) within each of the three realms. The fetter of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists of eighteen objects, meaning twelve objects as four categories within each of the three realms.

The fetter of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of six objects, being abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) within each of the three realms. The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) consists of three [objects].

The four categories of each realm constitute twelve matters. The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) each belong to the desire realm and are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), thus constituting two matters.

If categorized according to the seventy-five dharmas, the first three and the seventh take as their nature greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) within the indeterminate stages (*aniyata-bhūmi*).
The fourth takes as its nature ignorance (*avidyā*) among the great afflictions (*kleśa*). The fifth and sixth take as their nature [the remaining] great...
Among the dharmas of the ground, wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes the nature of the latter two [fetters]; among the minor afflictions, envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) constitute their nature.

Because they bind sentient beings so that they do not emerge from the triple world (*tridhātu*), they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*). Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*):

to the seven stations of consciousness (*saptavijñānasthitayaḥ*), one adds the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattvāḥ*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); with these added, there are nine. It is only within these that all classes of sentient beings reside.
The nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*) are established because they are dwellings of joyful delight; other places are not so established because they are not dwellings of joyful delight.

Their essential nature should be understood according to the explanation of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), with the addition of the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the points of difference. Regarding the nine levels (*bhūmi*):

these refer to the desire realm, the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). "Level" refers to the basis [of existence]; in the realms of desire and form, its nature consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The four aggregates of the formless realm, the desire realm, the form realm, and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*). Among the seventy-five dharmas—

excluding the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas from within the seventy-two dharmas— the eleven material dharmas, the odors and tastes, the two types of secondary afflictions belonging to the ground of the unwholesome (*akuśala-bhūmika*),

and among the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), vexation (*pradāśa*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), resentment (*upanāha*), and the indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors [are included].

Among the dissociated [factors], sleep (*middha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), and anger (*vyāpāda*) belong only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) belong only to the fourth dhyāna;
the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as guile (*śāṭhya*) and deceit (*māyā*) belong only to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Among the indeterminate [factors], vitarka and vicāra belong only to the desire realm and the first dhyāna. Regarding the dissociated factors of name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*), if one speaks according to the language, they belong to the desire realm and the first dhyāna.

Regarding concentration (*samādhi*): if one speaks of it as being associated with the body, it is found in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four dhyānas; among the eleven types of matter (*rūpa*), it is present in the five faculties (eye, etc.), matter, sound, and tangibles;

and among the non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter, it is present in the desire realm and the four dhyānas. Regarding the mind-king (*cittarāja*), it is associated with the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), the ten great afflictive mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—specifically pride (*māna*) within the category of "minor" afflictions—and greed (*lobha*), conceit (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) within the category of "indeterminate" factors, as well as acquisition (*prāpti*) within the category of "factors dissociated from mind."
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) are present in nine stages (*bhūmi*).

As for the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), they refer to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), which arise in succession; thus, they are called "successive attainments.

Because these are the meritorious qualities of the noble ones (*ārya*), they are exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*); the four dhyānas have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their nature, while the four formless attainments have the four aggregates as their nature.
The nature of the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling consists solely of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

If one considers it within the context of the seventy-five dharmas, its essence is comprised of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the mind-king (*citta*), the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the ten great wholesome ground factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), the two [mental factors of] vitarka and vicāra, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of acquisition (*prāpti*), and so forth;

this constitutes the first dhyāna. For the latter three dhyānas, vitarka and vicāra are excluded, while the rest are as described for the first dhyāna. Furthermore, for the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), these are likewise excluded.

Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is as previously explained for the first dhyāna. The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) has the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) as its essence.

Regarding the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*): first, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the desire realm; second, that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation in the desire realm; third, that which is abandoned through the vision of the path in the desire realm;

fourth, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the form and formless realms; fifth, that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation in the form and formless realms... [and so forth].
It should be understood that one full comprehension (*parijñā*) is established for the six [defilements] abandoned through the path of seeing in the form and formless realms;

another is established for the seven [defilements] abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm—this being the full comprehension of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), as it was established previously;

a further full comprehension is established for those abandoned through the path of cultivation in the form realm—this being the full comprehension of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā-kṣaya-parijñā*); and [finally], for the formless realm...

Regarding the single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) established for that which is abandoned through the path of cultivation: it is the thorough knowledge of the eternal exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

This is also combined with the preceding [thorough knowledges] to establish a single [category]. Thus, these nine thorough knowledges have analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as their intrinsic nature. They are called "thorough knowledges" because the name of the cause is applied to the fruit.

The analysis according to ten categories consists briefly of six types: the ten *paryavasthānas*, the ten *anuśayas*, the ten paths of wholesome action, the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*, the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), and the ten powers (*bala*).
Regarding the ten *paryavasthānas*: first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); second, lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*); third, envy (*īrṣyā*); fourth, avarice (*mātsarya*);

fifth, regret (*kaukṛtya*); sixth, sleep (*middha*); seventh, restlessness (*auddhatya*); eighth, lethargy (*styāna*); ninth, anger (*krodha*); and tenth, concealment (*mrakṣa*). They are called *paryavasthānas* because they bind sentient beings.

The first two [of the ten minor afflictions] belong to the great unwholesome ground; envy (*īrṣyā*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) belong to the group of minor afflictions;

remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) belong to the two indeterminate factors; and restlessness (*auddhatya*) and lethargy (*styāna*) belong to the two factors of the great affliction ground. Regarding the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*): first, attachment (*rāga*); second, aversion (*pratigha*);
third, pride (*māna*); fourth, doubt (*vicikitsā*); fifth, ignorance (*avidyā*); sixth, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); seventh, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The eight wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the nine grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the ten grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are "latent" (*anuśaya*); "latent" means they follow along and adhere.

Because their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle, they are called "latencies. If categorized according to the three realms and five classes [of afflictions], these ten have a total of ninety-eight entities as their substance, as explained for the first seven fetters (*saṃyojana*) among the nine fetters;
the only difference is that stinginess (*mātsarya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*) are excluded. If categorized according to the seven... [text ends]
Among the fifteen factors, the first four have greed, hatred, pride, and doubt—taken from the indeterminate factors—as their substance;
ignorance has the ignorance found among the universal defiled mental factors as its nature; and the latter five views have wisdom—taken from the universal mental factors—as their nature.
The ten paths of wholesome action are: first, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from taking what is not given; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct;
fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from harsh speech; sixth, abstaining from divisive speech; seventh, abstaining from frivolous speech;

eighth, non-attachment; ninth, non-hatred; and tenth, right view. Of these, the first three are in nature informative and non-informative bodily actions (*kāyakarma-vijñapti-avijñapti*), while the [next] four are vocal actions (*vākkarma*).

The nature of the three final paths of action of the mind (*manas-karmapatha*) is non-manifestation (*avijñapti*). Bodily manifestation has as its nature matter (*rūpa*) among the eleven types of matter;
vocal manifestation has sound (*śabda*) as its nature; and both bodily and vocal non-manifestation have non-manifestation as their nature.

Non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*) have as their nature non-attachment and non-hatred among the great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*); right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) has as its nature wisdom (*prajñā*) among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

The ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) are: (1) earth, (2) water, (3) fire, (4) wind, (5) blue, (6) yellow, (7) red, (8) white, (9) the sphere of infinite space, and (10) the sphere of infinite consciousness.
They are called "spheres of totality" because one observes earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth as being all-pervasive.
Among these ten, the first eight—like the pure deliverances (*śuddhavimokṣa*)—have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their essential nature, provided that their associated factors are included.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute their nature. Relying upon the fourth *dhyāna*, they take the desire realm as their object; among the intermediate [realms], they perceive visible forms, and among the latter two *āyatanas*, they are like the two purities of space and consciousness.
They have the four aggregates excluding consciousness as their nature, each taking the four aggregates of themselves and others as their objective domain.

Among the seventy-five dharmas, the first eight consist of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), and the ten great wholesome ground factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Regarding their nature, the latter two exclude the unmanifest (*avijñapti*); the rest are as previously stated. All eight are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

As for the ten knowledges (*jñāna*): first, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); second, dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*); third, subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); fourth, knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*); fifth, knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*); sixth, knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); seventh, knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*);

eighth, knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); ninth, knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*); and tenth, knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). [The first] is called conventional because it mostly takes conventional objects such as jars and so forth.

That which is named conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) takes the four truths of the desire realm as its object; that which is named dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) takes the four truths of the form and formless realms as its object.
Because it is the first to realize and know the true reality of all phenomena, it is called dharma-knowledge.

Subsequent objects and cognitions are similar to this preceding one, and thus receive the name "subsequent" (*anvaya*). Because they are realized in accordance with what preceded them, these preceding dharmas and subsequent [knowledges] arise by way of their respective objects.

Because they take as their respective objects the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, these are called the four knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. Because they know the minds of others, they are called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

These six knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—if they are comprised within the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and are not of the nature of views (*darśana*), are called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
This is because they arise simultaneously with the first attainment of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-prāpti*).
It is called "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) because [defilements] will not arise again, and it is called "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) for the same reason.

All ten knowledges have wisdom (*prajñā*) from among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as their essential nature. Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*): first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*) has all ten knowledges as its nature.

For example, that a virtuous cause produces a desirable result is termed "possible" (*sthāna*); that a virtuous cause produces an undesirable result is termed "impossible" (*asthāna*). Wisdom is able to know this.

The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) consists of eight knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
The power of knowing the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*) consists of eight knowledges, as it knows that such a type of karma brings about such a type of maturation.

The power of knowing the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments (*dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti-jñānabala*) consists of these four dhyānas, eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), three concentrations (*samādhi*), and eight attainments (*samāpatti*).

The "powers of knowledge" (*jñānabala*) are as follows: the power of knowing meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—which are synonyms for concentration—is the power of knowing meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and so forth, insofar as it can know those four dhyānas and the like.

The power of knowing the superiority and inferiority of the faculties (*indriya*) is the power of knowing the distinctions between the superior and inferior states of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the others.
The power of knowing the various inclinations (*adhimukti*) is the power of knowing the differences in the various inclinations and intentions of sentient beings.

The alternative names are: (5) the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*) and (6) the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*).
Knowing the various elemental natures of classes of sentient beings is called the power of knowledge regarding the various elements.

These four powers above all possess the nature of nine knowledges (*jñāna*), excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), because concentration, faculties, inclinations, and elements all pertain to the three [truths] of suffering, origin, and the path; therefore, these four powers all have the nature of nine knowledges and do not take [the truth of cessation] as their object.

Because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it excludes the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). The power of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*) consists of all nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation.

It is called the "knowledge of the paths leading everywhere" because it knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are capable of leading to their respective fruits; knowing these paths leading everywhere is the power of the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere.

If it takes the path that leads as its object (*ālambana*), it consists of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation; if it also takes the destination reached as its object, it consists of ten knowledges. Regarding the power of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-bala*), it is of the nature of eight knowledges.
The power of knowledge through recollection (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*) consists of knowing past deeds performed in former lives;
because this recollection is powerful, it is specifically designated here as "recollection" (*anusmṛti*), meaning the recollection of events according to their sequence.

The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānabala*) consists of knowing future births—dying here and being born there—and is thus called the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth. These two powers above are both observations of phenomena (*vastu*).
Furthermore, regarding the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the ten powers of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-bala*):

if one maintains that they take only the destruction of the outflows as their object, then six knowledges constitute them—excluding the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

If, however, one maintains that they consist of the ten knowledges attained within the body of one who has destroyed the outflows, then all ten powers have wisdom (*prajñā*) from among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) as their essential nature. For the sake of beginners, I have briefly indicated these general directions; the details [should be sought elsewhere].
The detailed analysis is as found in the separate record.
This concludes the "Source of the Dharma School."
